Theoretical Microeconomics

A complete reading on consumer and producer theory, choice under uncertainty, general equilibrium and the welfare theorems, game theory, information economics and mechanism design. These topics are usually split across several courses and can feel like a pile of unrelated theorems. So every chapter first says what question is being asked and why it is modelled this way, then gives definitions, theorems and proof ideas, and finally computes the result on the simplest possible example.

Prerequisites: multivariable calculus, basic linear algebra, introductory probability, and a little real analysis (compactness, continuity). Convex analysis and fixed-point theorems are explained when they are used.

What this text will let you do

After reading you should be able to:

  1. Solve a consumer's or a firm's problem by hand: find the best bundle for a given budget, the cheapest way to produce a given output, and read off how demand and supply respond to prices (Chapters 1–4).
  2. Find the prices that clear the markets of a small economy and check by hand whether the outcome is efficient (Chapters 5–6).
  3. Solve a small game: find dominant strategies, Nash equilibria (pure and mixed) and subgame perfect equilibria by backward induction (Chapters 7–9).
  4. Explain with numbers why hidden information distorts contracts and markets: adverse selection, signalling, screening, moral hazard (Chapter 10).
  5. Design a simple rule (an auction with a reserve price, a menu of contracts) and say why truth-telling can be made optimal (Chapter 11).

How to read.

  • Every chapter opens with a box Intuition: the question the chapter answers, in plain words. Read these first; they carry the story.
  • Each core idea is followed by a Worked example with round numbers. Do the arithmetic yourself; every step is shown.
  • Paragraphs that start with Proof can be skipped on a first reading. Each important proof is preceded by a one-sentence summary (In one sentence), so you know why the result holds without following the details.
  • Sections marked Advanced go beyond what later chapters need; skip them freely.
  • The last three chapters collect common misconceptions, exercises with answers and a glossary.

Notation and overview

  • x\in\mathbb R^n_+ is a consumption bundle, p\in\mathbb R^n_{++} prices, I income, \succsim preferences, U a utility function.
  • y\in\mathbb R^n is a production plan (positive = output, negative = input), f a production function, w input prices.
  • x\gg0 means every component is strictly positive, x\ge y means componentwise \ge. \nabla U is the gradient.
  • In games s_i is a pure strategy, \sigma_i a mixed strategy, s_{-i} the strategies of everyone but i.
  • Proofs end with \square.

0. The Big Picture: What Is Microeconomics About?

0.1 One thread: optimisation, equilibrium, efficiency

Three connected questions organise everything:

  1. Individual optimisation. Given constraints, what does a rational agent choose? (Consumers choose bundles, firms inputs and outputs, players strategies, principals contracts.)
  2. Equilibrium. When everyone optimises at once and choices affect one another, which states are stable? (Prices that clear markets, strategies that are mutual best responses, beliefs consistent with strategies.)
  3. Efficiency and design. Is the equilibrium good? Can the rules be changed? (The welfare theorems say competitive equilibria are efficient, but they fail with externalities, public goods and asymmetric information; mechanism design asks the reverse: can we design rules whose equilibrium is the outcome we want?)

Intuition. Picture a town market. Everybody arrives with an "endowment": some have apples, some oranges, and everyone has tastes. If each person trades according to taste and budget, prices adjust until planned purchases equal planned sales. Could anyone now be made better off without hurting someone else? That is general equilibrium and the welfare theorems. If traders instead guess one another's moves and haggle, we are in game theory; if a seller does not know buyers' true valuations, we are in information economics and mechanism design.

0.2 The toolbox

Tool Where it is used In one sentence
Weierstrass (maximum) theorem existence of optimal choices a continuous function on a compact set attains its maximum
Lagrange / Kuhn–Tucker constrained optimisation the multiplier is the constraint's "shadow price"
Envelope theorem Roy's identity, Shephard's and Hotelling's lemmas the derivative of the optimal value equals the partial derivative of the objective
Duality utility maximisation vs expenditure minimisation one indifference curve, two ways of asking
Separating hyperplane second welfare theorem, social planner two disjoint convex sets can be separated by a line
Brouwer / Kakutani fixed points existence of general equilibrium and Nash equilibrium a continuous map of a compact convex set into itself has a fixed point
Backward induction / one-shot deviation dynamic games solve from the end; only check one-step deviations
Revelation principle mechanism design any mechanism's equilibrium can be replicated by a truthful direct mechanism

0.3 Three running examples and a road map

Three small examples return again and again.

Example Where What it shows
Alice's budget: she has 100 to spend on two goods with prices 2 and 5 Chapters 1–4 choice, demand, response to a price change
A two-person market: Alice and Bob swap apples and oranges Chapters 5–6 prices that clear markets, efficiency, redistribution
Two firms in one market; a seller who does not know the buyer Chapters 7–11 strategy, credibility, hidden information, rule design
Stage Question Everyday analogy Chapters
Optimisation what does one person choose? you in a supermarket with a budget 1–4
Equilibrium what is stable when everyone chooses at once? a market where prices settle 5, 7–9
Efficiency is the outcome good? could anyone gain without hurting others? 6
Information and design what if some know more? who writes the rules? buying a used car; designing an auction 10–11

A sense of scale. The examples are deliberately tiny: two goods, two people, two types. That is not because the world is that simple but because with two of everything every step can be computed by hand, and the logic carries over unchanged to many goods and many people.

1. Preferences and Utility

Intuition. Microeconomics does not start from "utility" but from something plainer: a person can say which of two options they prefer. A utility function is just a convenient way of writing that ranking as numbers. This chapter asks which rankings can be represented by a numerical function, whether that function is unique, and what its shape (monotone, quasi-concave) says about the preferences.

1.1 Binary relations and orders

A binary relation R on X is a subset of X\times X; (x,y)\in R is written xRy. Usual properties:

  • reflexive: xRx; transitive: xRy and yRz imply xRz;
  • complete: for any x,y, xRy or yRx;
  • symmetric: xRy\Rightarrow yRx; anti-symmetric: xRy and yRx imply x=y.

Reflexive + transitive is a preorder; transitive + anti-symmetric a partial order; a complete partial order is a linear order (any two points are comparable).

1.2 Preference relations

A consumer has preferences \succsim ("at least as good as") over bundles in X\subset\mathbb R^n_+ (non-empty, convex, compact, containing 0). They induce:

  • strict preference x\succ y: x\succsim y but not y\succsim x;
  • indifference x\sim y: x\succsim y and y\succsim x.

Useful sets: \succsim(x^0)=\{x:x\succsim x^0\} (at-least-as-good set), \precsim(x^0), \succ(x^0), \prec(x^0) and the indifference curve \sim(x^0)=\{x:x\sim x^0\}.

1.3 Axioms

Axiom Content Meaning
A1 Completeness any two bundles are comparable people can always choose
A2 Transitivity x\succsim y\succsim z\Rightarrow x\succsim z no cycles
A3 Continuity \succsim(x) and \precsim(x) are closed small changes do not flip rankings
A4′ Local non-satiation every neighbourhood of x contains a better bundle no bliss point
A4 Strict monotonicity y\ge x\Rightarrow y\succsim x; y\gg x\Rightarrow y\succ x more is better
A5′ Convexity y\succsim x\Rightarrow ty+(1-t)x\succsim x balanced bundles are liked
A5 Strict convexity strict version for y\ne x strictly prefers averages
A6 Homotheticity y\sim x\Rightarrow ty\sim tx doubling income scales choices

Complete and transitive preferences are called rational. Strict monotonicity implies local non-satiation.

Why transitivity? Someone with x\succ y\succ z\succ x is a "money pump": pay a little for each swap and go round the cycle back to the start. Transitivity rules this out and guarantees a best element in every finite set:

Theorem (ranking). If \succsim satisfies A1 and A2, the elements of any finite set A can be ranked in a list.

Proof idea. Scan the set keeping the best bundle so far; replace it whenever a better one appears. By transitivity each new champion is at least as good as everything seen before. \square

Theorem (intermediate value). If \succsim is complete, transitive and continuous and y\succ x\succ z, there is t\in(0,1) with ty+(1-t)z\sim x.

Proof idea. Let T=\{t:ty+(1-t)z\succsim x\} and t_0=\inf T. If the bundle at t_0 were strictly better or worse than x, openness of \succ(x) or \prec(x) would give a point contradicting the infimum; so it is indifferent. \square

Worked example (a money pump). Suppose someone prefers an apple to a banana, a banana to a cherry, and a cherry to an apple (a cycle), and would pay 1 to swap to a preferred fruit. Give them a banana: they pay 1 to swap it for the apple, 1 to swap the apple for the cherry, and 1 to swap the cherry for the banana. They are back where they started and 3 poorer. Transitivity rules this out.

Worked example (a ranking with no utility function). Compare bundles lexicographically: the bundle with more of good 1 always wins, however much of good 2 the other has; only a tie in good 1 is broken by good 2. So (2,0)\succ(1,100). Completeness, transitivity and monotonicity all hold, but no utility function represents these preferences: there are as many indifference classes as there are real numbers x_1, and no continuous function can separate them. The theorem therefore needs continuity.

1.4 Existence of a utility function

A function U:\mathbb R^n_+\to\mathbb R represents the preferences if U(x)\ge U(y)\iff x\succsim y.

Theorem. If preferences are complete, transitive, continuous and strictly monotone, a continuous utility function representing them exists.

The idea of the construction. Take the diagonal e=(1,\dots,1). For any bundle x find a "standard bundle" te with x\sim te and set U(x)=t. Strict monotonicity makes the number unique (further along the diagonal is better); continuity makes it exist.

In one sentence. Score a bundle by how far along the diagonal e=(1,\dots,1) you must go to find a bundle equally good; monotonicity makes this number unique and continuity makes it exist.

Proof sketch. (i) Existence: A=\{t\ge0:te\succsim x\} and B=\{t\ge0:te\precsim x\} are closed, monotone (upward/downward intervals) and by completeness cover the half-line, so they meet. (ii) Uniqueness: if t_0<t_1 were both indifferent to x, strict monotonicity gives t_0e\prec t_1e, a contradiction. (iii) Representation: U(x)e\sim x\succsim y\sim U(y)e. (iv) Continuity: U^{-1}(a,b)=\succ(ae)\cap\prec(be) is open. \square

Marginal notions. Marginal utility MU_i=\partial U/\partial x_i; marginal rate of substitution MRS_{ij}=MU_i/MU_j (how much j one will give up for one more unit of i); elasticity of substitution \sigma_{ij}=\dfrac{d\ln(x_i/x_j)}{d\ln(U_j/U_i)}.

1.5 Properties of utility functions

  • Ordinality. If U represents some preferences, so does V iff V=g(U) with g strictly increasing. Utility numbers have no meaning; only the ordering does.
  • U strictly increasing ⟺ strictly monotone preferences; U quasi-concave ⟺ convex preferences; strictly quasi-concave ⟺ strictly convex.
  • Homothetic preferences ⟺ utility can be chosen homogeneous of degree one. (Doubling income scales the optimal bundle; indifference curves are radial blow-ups of each other.)

Examples. Cobb–Douglas U=x_1^ax_2^{1-a} is strictly monotone, strictly quasi-concave and homothetic. CES U=(\alpha x_1^\rho+(1-\alpha)x_2^\rho)^{1/\rho} has \sigma=1/(1-\rho): \rho\to1 perfect substitutes, \rho\to0 Cobb–Douglas, \rho\to-\infty perfect complements (Leontief).

Worked example (Alice's tastes). Take U(x_1,x_2)=\sqrt{x_1x_2}. The bundles (4,1), (2,2) and (1,4) all give U=2: Alice is indifferent among them, so they lie on one indifference curve. The bundle (3,3) gives U=3>2 and is better than all three. Squaring gives V=U^2=x_1x_2, with the numbers 4 and 9 instead of 2 and 3; every pairwise ranking is unchanged, so V represents the same preferences. By contrast W=x_1+x_2 does not: it gives 5 to (4,1) and 4 to (2,2), although Alice is indifferent between them.

The marginal rate of substitution is MRS=U_1/U_2=x_2/x_1. At (4,1) it equals \tfrac14: she would give up only a quarter unit of good 2 for one more unit of good 1, because she already has a lot of good 1. At (2,2) it is 1 and at (1,4) it is 4. The MRS falls as she moves along the curve to more of good 1: the curve bows towards the origin (convex preferences).

2. Consumer Theory

Intuition. This chapter is the engine of microeconomics. The consumer asks two mirror-image questions: (1) given a budget, what is the most satisfying bundle? (utility maximisation, UMP) and (2) to reach a given satisfaction, what is the cheapest bundle? (expenditure minimisation, EMP). The answers look different but tell the same story (duality). From this duality we derive how demand responds to price (the Slutsky equation), and whether demand data alone can reveal rational preferences (integrability and revealed preference).

2.1 Utility maximisation

Assumption. U is continuous, strictly increasing and strictly quasi-concave; p\gg0, I>0. Budget set B=\{x\ge0:p\cdot x\le I\}.

\max_{x\ge0}\ U(x)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad p\cdot x\le I.

Theorem. A solution exists, is unique, and exhausts the budget.

In one sentence. The budget set is closed and bounded, so a best bundle exists; two best bundles would have a strictly better average, so it is unique; and an unspent dollar could always buy a little more, so the whole budget is spent.

Proof. The budget set is compact and U continuous, so a maximum exists. Two solutions x^1\ne x^2 would have a feasible convex combination of strictly higher utility (strict quasi-concavity). If p\cdot x<I, strictly increasing U allows buying a bit more. \square

Solution. Lagrangian L=U(x)+\lambda(I-p\cdot x)+\mu\cdot x; Kuhn–Tucker conditions

U_i(x)=\lambda p_i-\mu_i,\qquad \lambda(I-p\cdot x)=0,\qquad\mu_ix_i=0.
An interior solution satisfies \dfrac{U_i}{U_j}=\dfrac{p_i}{p_j}: the marginal rate of substitution equals the price ratio (indifference curve tangent to the budget line), and \lambda=U_i/p_i is the marginal utility of a dollar.

Kuhn–Tucker theorem (sufficiency). If U is strictly quasi-concave and differentiable, (p,I)\gg0, and (x^*,\lambda^*)\gg0 satisfies the first-order conditions, then x^* solves the problem. (Quasi-concavity makes local optima global.)

The solution x^*(p,I) is the Marshallian demand; the price elasticity is \epsilon_i=\partial\ln x_i^*/\partial\ln p_i.

Example (Cobb–Douglas). U=x_1^ax_2^{1-a}: the first-order condition gives \dfrac{a\,x_2}{(1-a)\,x_1}=\dfrac{p_1}{p_2}; with the budget,

x_1^*=\frac{aI}{p_1},\qquad x_2^*=\frac{(1-a)I}{p_2}.
Each good gets a fixed budget share (a and 1-a), independent of prices.

Worked example (Alice's budget). Alice has U=x_1^{0.4}x_2^{0.6}, income I=100 and prices p=(2,5). By the Cobb–Douglas formula

x_1^*=\frac{0.4\cdot100}{2}=20,\qquad x_2^*=\frac{0.6\cdot100}{5}=12.
Budget: 2\cdot20+5\cdot12=40+60=100. Tangency: MRS=\dfrac{0.4\,x_2}{0.6\,x_1}=\dfrac{0.4\cdot12}{0.6\cdot20}=0.4=\dfrac{p_1}{p_2}=\dfrac25. Her utility is U=20^{0.4}\,12^{0.6}\approx14.72, and one more unit of money is worth \lambda=U_1/p_1\approx0.147 units of utility (checked in the next section).

Worked example (corners and kinks). Not every problem has a tangency. With perfect complements U=\min(x_1,x_2) (left and right shoes) Alice buys equal amounts, x_1=x_2=I/(p_1+p_2)=100/7\approx14.3; the MRS plays no role. With perfect substitutes U=x_1+x_2 she spends everything on the cheaper good.

2.2 The indirect utility function

Definition. V(p,I)=U(x^*(p,I)), optimal utility as a function of prices and income.

Theorem (properties). If U is continuous and strictly increasing, V(p,I) is:

  1. continuous;
  2. homogeneous of degree zero in (p,I) (scaling both leaves the budget set unchanged);
  3. strictly increasing in I;
  4. decreasing in p;
  5. quasi-convex in (p,I);
  6. Roy's identity: if differentiable with \partial V/\partial I\ne0, x_i^*(p,I)=-\dfrac{\partial V/\partial p_i}{\partial V/\partial I}.

Proof of Roy's identity (envelope theorem). The derivative of a value function equals the partial derivative of the Lagrangian: \partial V/\partial p_i=-\lambda x_i, \partial V/\partial I=\lambda; divide. Intuition: a price rise of one unit costs welfare equal to the multiplier times the quantity you were buying.

Quasi-convexity idea. The union of two budget sets always contains the budget set at the averaged prices and income, so the averaged problem cannot beat the better of the two. \square

Worked example (value function and Roy's identity). For Cobb–Douglas, V(p,I)=0.5102\,\dfrac{I}{p_1^{0.4}p_2^{0.6}}, where 0.5102=0.4^{0.4}\,0.6^{0.6}. At p=(2,5), I=100: V\approx14.72. Then \partial V/\partial I=V/I=0.1472 (this is \lambda: one more unit of money raises utility by 0.147) and \partial V/\partial p_1=-0.4\,V/p_1=-2.944. Roy's identity gives x_1=2.944/0.1472=20, as before. Homogeneity of degree zero: doubling prices and income together, p=(4,10), I=200, gives the same V\approx14.72.

2.3 Expenditure minimisation

\min_{x\ge0}\ p\cdot x\quad\text{s.t.}\quad U(x)\ge U_0.

The solution x^H(p,U) is the Hicksian (compensated) demand; the minimal outlay e(p,U)=p\cdot x^H(p,U) is the expenditure function.

Theorem (properties). If U is continuous, strictly increasing and strictly quasi-concave:

  1. e=0 at the lowest utility level;
  2. continuous;
  3. for p\gg0 strictly increasing and unbounded in U;
  4. increasing in p;
  5. homogeneous of degree one in p;
  6. concave in p;
  7. Shephard's lemma: \dfrac{\partial e}{\partial p_i}=x_i^H(p,U).

Intuition for concavity. When prices change the consumer can re-optimise. If he could not (holding the old bundle), expenditure would be linear in prices; being able to adjust makes it grow more slowly, so e is concave in p.

Proof of concavity. Let \bar p=tp^1+(1-t)p^2 and \bar x=x^H(\bar p,U_0). At prices p^1,p^2 the bundle \bar x still achieves U_0, so p^k\bar x\ge e(p^k,U_0); take the weighted sum: e(\bar p,U_0)\ge te(p^1,U_0)+(1-t)e(p^2,U_0). \square

Shephard's lemma is again the envelope theorem: \partial e/\partial p_i=\partial L/\partial p_i=x_i^H. Intuition: if a price rises by one, holding satisfaction fixed costs exactly the amount you were buying.

Worked example (expenditure and Hicksian demand). For Cobb–Douglas the expenditure function is e(p,U)=U\,p_1^{0.4}p_2^{0.6}/0.5102. To reach Alice's utility 14.72 at p=(2,5) one needs e=14.72\times3.4658/0.5102\approx100, exactly her income: the two problems are mirror images (duality, next section). Shephard's lemma: x_1^H=\partial e/\partial p_1=0.4\,e/p_1=0.4\cdot100/2=20, again her demand.

2.4 Duality

Lemma. e(p,V(p,I))\le I and V(p,e(p,U))\ge U.

Theorem (duality). If U is continuous and strictly increasing,

e(p,V(p,I))=I,\qquad V(p,e(p,U))=U.
If U is also strictly quasi-concave, x^*(p,I)=x^H(p,V(p,I)) and x^H(p,U)=x^*(p,e(p,U)).

In one sentence. If one problem could be solved more cheaply than the other claims, the first problem could be improved too, contradicting its optimality.

Proof (contradiction). If e(p,V(p,I_0))<I_0, continuity lets us raise utility slightly while still spending less than I_0, contradicting optimality of V. The other direction is symmetric. \square

Intuition. Picture the tangency of an indifference curve and a budget line. "Find the highest curve for a given budget" and "find the lowest budget for a given curve" yield the same tangency point. So Marshallian demand (income held fixed) and Hicksian demand (utility held fixed) coincide there and differ only in how they respond when prices move.

2.5 The Slutsky equation

Theorem. For all i,j:

\underbrace{\frac{\partial x_i(p,I)}{\partial p_j}}_{\text{total effect}}=\underbrace{\frac{\partial x_i^H(p,U)}{\partial p_j}}_{\text{substitution effect}}\;\underbrace{-\,x_j(p,I)\frac{\partial x_i(p,I)}{\partial I}}_{\text{income effect}}.

Proof. From duality x_i^H(p,U)=x_i^*(p,e(p,U)); differentiate with respect to p_j and use Shephard's lemma \partial e/\partial p_j=x_j. \square

Intuition. Bread becomes more expensive. You do two things: (1) bread is relatively dearer so you switch to other goods (the substitution effect, which always lowers demand for the good since it is measured at constant satisfaction); (2) you are effectively poorer (the income effect, whose sign depends on whether bread is normal or inferior).

  • Normal good \partial x_i/\partial I>0; inferior good \partial x_i/\partial I<0; Giffen good: demand rises with its own price (\partial x_i/\partial p_i>0). A Giffen good must be inferior with an income effect large enough to beat the substitution effect (staple food for very poor households).

Example. For Cobb–Douglas \partial x_1^*/\partial p_1=-aI/p_1^2. The income effect is -x_1\,\partial x_1/\partial I=-\dfrac{aI}{p_1}\cdot\dfrac a{p_1}, so the substitution effect is -\dfrac{aI}{p_1^2}+\dfrac{a^2I}{p_1^2}=-\dfrac{a(1-a)I}{p_1^2}<0.

Worked example (a price rise, in numbers). Alice's price p_1 rises from 2 to 2.5 (+25%).

  • Total effect. She now buys x_1=0.4\cdot100/2.5=16, down from 20: a change of -4.
  • Substitution effect. How much money would restore her old utility 14.72 at the new price? e'=100\times1.25^{0.4}\approx109.34. With that budget her Hicksian demand is x_1^H=0.4\cdot109.34/2.5\approx17.49: a change of -2.51. (She switches towards good 2, whose Hicksian demand rises from 12 to 0.6\cdot109.34/5\approx13.12.)
  • Income effect. Taking the extra 9.34 away again moves her from 17.49 to 16: a change of -1.49.

Check: -2.51-1.49=-4. Both effects lower the demand for good 1 because it is a normal good for her.

2.6 Properties of demand and the Slutsky matrix

Theorem. Marshallian demand is homogeneous of degree zero and satisfies budget balance p\cdot x^*=I; Hicksian demand is homogeneous of degree zero in p and exhausts the utility constraint.

Slutsky matrix: S(p,I)=\Big[\dfrac{\partial x_i}{\partial p_j}+x_j\dfrac{\partial x_i}{\partial I}\Big]_{ij}.

Theorem. S is symmetric and negative semi-definite, and S(p,I)\,p=0.

In one sentence. The Slutsky matrix is the Hessian (matrix of second derivatives) of the expenditure function, and a Hessian is symmetric and, for a concave function, negative semi-definite.

Proof. By Slutsky's equation S=[\partial x_i^H/\partial p_j], which by Shephard's lemma is [\partial^2e/\partial p_i\partial p_j], the Hessian of the expenditure function: Young's theorem gives symmetry, concavity of e gives negative semi-definiteness. Sp=0 follows from homogeneity and budget balance via Euler's theorem. \square

Implications (testable): compensated own-price demand slopes down (\partial x^H_i/\partial p_i\le0); cross-substitution effects are symmetric (\partial x^H_i/\partial p_j=\partial x^H_j/\partial p_i).

Worked example (the Slutsky matrix is symmetric). For Cobb–Douglas, \partial x_1/\partial p_2=0 and \partial x_1/\partial I=a/p_1, so S_{12}=x_2\,a/p_1=a(1-a)I/(p_1p_2). Likewise S_{21}=x_1(1-a)/p_2=a(1-a)I/(p_1p_2). They are equal. With Alice's numbers S_{12}=S_{21}=12\cdot0.4/2=2.4. The Marshallian cross-price effects are zero, yet the compensated cross effects are positive: once the income effect is removed the two goods are substitutes.

2.7 Integrability: from demand back to preferences

Advanced section: it explains how demand data can be turned back into preferences. Skip it on a first reading.

Intuition. So far: preferences → demand. In practice we see demand, not preferences. Integrability asks: when does a given demand function come from rational preferences? The answer: exactly when it has the necessary properties above — budget balance and a symmetric, negative semi-definite Slutsky matrix.

Recovering utility from the expenditure function. For any e(p,u) with the seven properties define

u(x)=\max\{u\ge U(0):\ p\cdot x\ge e(p,u)\ \forall p\gg0\}.
It is well defined, unbounded, increasing and quasi-concave, and the expenditure function it generates is e (the verification theorem).

Intuition: x costs at least e(p,u) at every price, so it can reach u; the largest such u is its utility. Numerically u(x)=\max_u\min_p[p\cdot x-e(p,u)] (attained at 0).

Recovering the expenditure function from demand. If x(p,I) satisfies budget balance and its Slutsky matrix is symmetric, it is homogeneous of degree zero in p (symmetry is stronger than homogeneity).

Integrability theorem. A differentiable x(p,I) satisfying budget balance with a symmetric, negative semi-definite Slutsky matrix is the demand generated by some increasing, quasi-concave utility.

Proof idea. Treat \partial e/\partial p_i=x_i(p,e) as a system of partial differential equations. Symmetry of the Slutsky matrix gives the integrability (Frobenius/Young) condition, so a solution exists; negative semi-definiteness makes e concave in p; budget balance plus Euler's theorem gives degree-one homogeneity. Then recover u as above. \square

Example (two goods). With only two goods, budget balance and homogeneity of degree zero already imply a symmetric Slutsky matrix: differentiate the budget equation in p_1,p_2,I and apply Euler's theorem.

2.8 Revealed preference

Intuition. Preferences are invisible but choices are visible. If at prices p^1 you bought x^1 while x^2 was affordable, you "revealed" a preference for x^1. If at other prices p^2 you buy x^2 when x^1 was affordable, you contradict yourself.

WARP. If x^1\ne x^2, x^1 is chosen at p^1, x^2 at p^2, and p^1x^1\ge p^1x^2, then p^2x^1>p^2x^2.

SARP. The analogous condition for choice chains of any length (rules out cycles of any length).

Theorem. Budget balance + WARP imply homogeneity of degree zero and a negative semi-definite Slutsky matrix.

Proof idea. Take x^0=x(p^0,I^0) and the choice x^1 at p^1=p^0+tz with income just enough for x^0. WARP gives (p^0-p^1)(x^1-x^0)\ge0; differentiate f(t)=z\cdot x(p^0+tz,(p^0+tz)x^0) at t=0 to get z^TSz\le0. \square

Converse. If demand is homogeneous of degree zero, satisfies budget balance, and (p^1)^TS(p^0,I)p^1<0 for p^1 not proportional to p^0, then WARP holds.

Worked example (testing WARP on data). Two observations: at prices p^1=(1,2) Alice buys x^1=(4,2) (cost 8); at p^2=(1,3) she buys x^2=(2,3) (cost 11).

  • At p^1, x^2 would have cost 1\cdot2+2\cdot3=8\le8: it was affordable, so x^1 is revealed preferred to x^2.
  • At p^2, x^1 would have cost 1\cdot4+3\cdot2=10\le11: it was affordable, so x^2 is revealed preferred to x^1.

Each is preferred to the other: WARP is violated and no rational preference can produce this data. Change the second observation to p^2=(2,1), x^2=(2,4) (cost 8): now x^1 would cost 2\cdot4+1\cdot2=10>8, so the second choice says nothing against the first and WARP holds.

3. Choice under Uncertainty

Intuition. Until now every choice was "certain". In reality you choose lotteries: insurance, investments, a PhD. We want to extend preferences from bundles to probability distributions. The central question: under which axioms can preferences over lotteries be reduced to "compute an expected utility"? Why does a seemingly technical axiom (independence) matter so much? And how do we measure whether someone dislikes risk?

3.1 Lotteries and axioms

A simple lottery g=(p_1\circ a_1,\dots,p_n\circ a_n), p_i\ge0, \sum p_i=1, with outcomes a_i. In a compound lottery the prizes are themselves lotteries.

Axiom Content
G1–G3 completeness, reflexivity, transitivity (as in Chapter 1)
G4 Continuity every g is indifferent to a mixture (\alpha\circ a_1,(1-\alpha)\circ a_n) of best and worst outcomes
G4′ Archimedean if \pi\succ\rho\succ\sigma, some mixtures of \pi,\sigma are better and some worse than \rho (nothing is infinitely good or bad)
G5 Monotonicity a higher probability of the best outcome is better
G6 Substitution replacing a prize of a compound lottery with an indifferent prize leaves the lottery indifferent
G7 Reduction a compound lottery is indifferent to its induced simple lottery (only final probabilities matter, no fun in gambling)
G8 Independence \pi\sim\rho\iff\alpha\pi+(1-\alpha)\sigma\sim\alpha\rho+(1-\alpha)\sigma

G6 and G7 imply independence. Meaning of independence: mixing two lotteries with a common third one in the same proportion should not change how they compare — preferences are separable across states, which is the source of the expected-utility structure.

3.2 The expected utility theorem

Definition (vNM utility). U has the expected utility property if U(g)=\sum_ip_iU(a_i).

Theorem. If preferences satisfy G1–G7, a von Neumann–Morgenstern utility function representing them exists.

In one sentence. Score each prize by the chance of the best prize in an equally good "standard lottery"; replacing every prize by its standard lottery turns any lottery into one over the best and worst prizes only, and its best-prize probability is the expected score.

Construction. Let a_1 be the best and a_n the worst outcome. By continuity every lottery g has a unique U(g)\in[0,1] with g\sim(U(g)\circ a_1,(1-U(g))\circ a_n) (the probability in the "standard lottery" is the utility). Replace each prize a_i by its standard lottery; by substitution and reduction the compound lottery becomes a mixture of a_1 and a_n with probability \sum p_iU(a_i) of a_1, which is the expected-utility form. \square

Theorem (uniqueness). A vNM utility is unique up to a positive affine transformation: V=\alpha+\beta U, \beta>0. (Much stronger than Chapter 1's "any monotone transformation": expectation makes utility differences meaningful.)

Worked example (building a vNM utility). Outcomes 0, 50, 100. Set U(0)=0 and U(100)=1. Ask: for which \alpha is a sure 50 as good as "100 with probability \alpha, else 0"? Suppose \alpha=0.7; then U(50)=0.7. Every lottery over these prizes is now scored by its expected utility. For g=(0.2\circ0,\ 0.5\circ50,\ 0.3\circ100):

U(g)=0.2\cdot0+0.5\cdot0.7+0.3\cdot1=0.65,
so g is as good as a lottery giving 100 with probability 0.65. Since U(50)=0.7>0.5, utility is concave in money: risk aversion (next section).

Worked example (Allais: why independence is a real assumption). First choose between A: 1 million for sure, and B: 10% of 5 million, 89% of 1 million, 1% of nothing. Then choose between C: 11% of 1 million (else nothing), and D: 10% of 5 million (else nothing). Many people choose A and D. Under expected utility this pair of choices is impossible:

A\succ B\iff 0.11\,U(1)>0.1\,U(5)+0.01\,U(0),\qquad C\succ D\iff 0.11\,U(1)+0.89\,U(0)>0.1\,U(5)+0.9\,U(0),
and the two right-hand inequalities are the same. So expected utility says A\succB exactly when C\succD. People who choose A and D violate independence; expected utility is a very useful approximation, not a law of nature.

3.3 Attitudes to risk

Take a vNM utility U(w) over wealth (continuous, strictly increasing). Let \delta_\mu be the degenerate lottery paying the mean \mu=E_F[x] for sure.

  • Risk averse: \delta_\mu\succsim F for all F; risk loving: \precsim; risk neutral: \sim.
  • Certainty equivalent CE(F,U): U(CE)=\int U\,dF, the sure wealth indifferent to F.
  • Risk premium r(F,U)=\mu_F-CE(F,U): expected wealth sacrificed to avoid the risk.

Theorem. Equivalent: (1) risk averse; (2) U concave; (3) CE(F,U)\le\mu_F; (4) r\ge0.

Proof (1⇒2): apply risk aversion to two-point distributions to get concavity; (2⇒3) is Jensen: U(E[x])\ge E[U(x)]=U(CE). \square

Measures (Arrow–Pratt):

\text{absolute risk aversion }\lambda(x)=-\frac{U''(x)}{U'(x)},\qquad\text{relative risk aversion }R(x)=-\frac{xU''(x)}{U'(x)}.

Theorem. For two preferences the following are equivalent: (1) 1 is more risk averse than 2; (2) U_1=\phi(U_2) with \phi concave increasing; (3) CE(F,U_1)\le CE(F,U_2); (4) r_1\ge r_2; (5) \lambda_1(x)\ge\lambda_2(x).

Examples. CARA: U=-e^{-aw}, \lambda\equiv a. CRRA: U=w^{1-\gamma}/(1-\gamma), R\equiv\gamma. For a small risk with variance \sigma^2, r\approx\tfrac12\lambda(\mu)\sigma^2: risk premium \approx risk aversion × variance ÷ 2.

Worked example (risk premium). Take U(w)=\sqrt w and the gamble "wealth 0 or 100 with equal probability". Expected wealth =50; expected utility =\tfrac12\sqrt0+\tfrac12\sqrt{100}=5, so CE=5^2=25 and the risk premium is 50-25=25. For a small risk, wealth 90 or 110: E[U]=\tfrac12(9.4868+10.4881)=9.9875, CE=99.75, premium 0.25. Arrow–Pratt: \lambda(100)=-U''/U'=1/(2\cdot100)=0.005 and variance =100, so \tfrac12\lambda\sigma^2=0.25, exact to two decimals.

Worked example (why people insure). Wealth is 100; with probability \tfrac12 a loss of 36 occurs; U=\sqrt w. Without insurance E[U]=\tfrac12\sqrt{100}+\tfrac12\sqrt{64}=9, so CE=81, while expected wealth is 82. A fair full-insurance contract costs 18 (the expected loss) and leaves a sure 82>81, so she buys. The most she would pay is 19 (sure wealth 81), so the insurer can earn up to 1 on average. Risk aversion is the reason insurance exists.

3.4 Comparing gambles: stochastic dominance

  • First-order stochastic dominance (FOSD): F\succsim_{FOSD}G if \int UdF\ge\int UdG for every increasing U. Theorem: this holds iff F(x)\le G(x) for all x (F's distribution function lies below: the distribution is shifted right).

    Proof. By parts, \int U(dF-dG)=\int U'(x)(G(x)-F(x))dx. With U'\ge0 this is nonnegative for all U iff G\ge F; conversely test with step functions U=\mathbb 1\{x\ge x'\}. \square

  • Second-order stochastic dominance (SOSD): every increasing concave U prefers F. Equivalent: \int_{-\infty}^xF(t)dt\le\int_{-\infty}^xG(t)dt for all x. (F has no lower mean and less risk.)

Worked example (dominance). Let F give wealth 2 or 4 with probability \tfrac12 each and G give 1 or 4. F is G with the bad outcome improved, so every increasing U prefers F (FOSD); with U=\sqrt w: E_F=\tfrac12(1.414+2)=1.707>E_G=1.5. Next compare H: a sure 3, and K=F: 2 or 4 equally likely, with the same mean 3. No increasing U ranks them in general (a convex U prefers K), but every concave increasing U prefers H: H second-order dominates K (it is K without a mean-preserving spread). With U=\sqrt w: \sqrt3=1.732>1.707.

3.5 Subjective probability: the Anscombe–Aumann framework

Advanced section: it is a useful extension, but later chapters do not depend on it.

Probabilities so far were "objective". For weather or stock prices there are none. Anscombe–Aumann uses two layers: finitely many states s\in\Omega (no objective probabilities), and in each state a lottery over outcomes X (with objective probabilities). An act is h:\Omega\to\Delta X; a constant act has the same lottery in every state.

Mixture-space theorem. Preferences on a convex set are complete, transitive, independent and Archimedean iff they are represented by an affine function U, unique up to positive affine transformations. This yields U(h)=\sum_s\sum_xh_s(x)U_s(x) (state-dependent expected utility).

To read off subjective probabilities we need state independence: in non-null states (where changing the outcome affects preferences) the ranking of prize-lotteries does not depend on the state. State independence implies monotonicity.

Expected-utility theorem (AA). Preferences are independent, Archimedean and state independent iff there are a vNM utility U:X\to\mathbb R and subjective probabilities \mu(s) with

U(h)=\sum_s\mu(s)\sum_xh_s(x)U(x).

Intuition. Subjective probability is not an arbitrary belief; it is identified from choices: if you would give 3 dollars on "rain" for 1 dollar on "no rain", you put three times the weight on rain.

4. Producer Theory

Intuition. A firm asks questions very like the consumer's: how to produce a given amount at least cost (cost minimisation, like expenditure minimisation) and how to earn the most (profit maximisation, like utility maximisation). The mathematics is almost parallel: cost function ↔ expenditure function, Shephard's lemma ↔ same, Hotelling's lemma ↔ Roy's identity. We start with the most general description of technology, the production possibility set, and then specialise to a single-output production function.

4.1 The production possibility set

Advanced section: it describes technology in full generality. For the rest it is enough to know the production function of Section 4.2.

Y\subset\mathbb R^n; for y\in Y positive entries are outputs, negative entries inputs.

Property Meaning
No free lunch Y\cap\mathbb R^n_+\subset\{0\}: no inputs, no outputs
Possibility of inaction 0\in Y
Free disposal y\in Y, y'\le y ⟹ y'\in Y
Irreversibility y\in Y, y\ne0 ⟹ -y\notin Y
Non-increasing returns \alpha y\in Y for \alpha\in[0,1]
Non-decreasing returns \alpha y\in Y for \alpha\ge1
Constant returns (CRS) \alpha y\in Y for \alpha\ge0
Increasing / decreasing returns scaling up strictly feasible and down infeasible / the reverse
Additivity y,y'\in Y\Rightarrow y+y'\in Y
Convexity Y is convex
Convex cone \alpha y+\beta y'\in Y for \alpha,\beta\ge0

Theorem. (1) Y is additive with non-increasing returns iff it is a convex cone; (2) any convex Y\ni0 can be turned into a constant-returns set in \mathbb R^{n+1} by adding a hidden "entrepreneur" dimension — so CRS is not a real restriction of generality (profit accrues to the hidden fixed factor).

4.2 The production function

Single output: y=f(x), Y=\{(-x,y):y\le f(x)\}. Standard assumption: f is continuous, strictly increasing, strictly quasi-concave, f(0)=0. Isoquant Q(y)=\{x:f(x)=y\}.

Theorem. Returns to scale: CRS ⟺ f(tx)=tf(x); increasing ⟺ f(tx)>tf(x) (t>1); decreasing ⟺ f(tx)<tf(x); Y convex ⟺ f concave.

Separability. Partition inputs into groups K_1,\dots,K_s. Weak separability: the marginal rate of technical substitution f_i/f_j within a group is unaffected by inputs outside it ("a group can be aggregated into a sub-index"). Strong separability: even cross-group substitution rates depend only on the two groups involved.

4.3 Cost minimisation

C(w,y)=\min_{x\ge0}\ w\cdot x\quad\text{s.t.}\quad f(x)\ge y.

Mathematically identical to expenditure minimisation, so cost-function properties mirror those of e: C(w,0)=0; continuous; strictly increasing and unbounded in y; increasing, degree-one homogeneous and concave in w; Shephard's lemma \partial C/\partial w_i=x_i(w,y) (conditional factor demands). The first-order condition w_i=\lambda f_i(x) says marginal rate of technical substitution = input price ratio; the multiplier \lambda=\partial C/\partial y is marginal cost.

Conditional factor demands are homogeneous of degree zero in w, and the substitution matrix [\partial x_i/\partial w_j] is symmetric and negative semi-definite (own-price effects non-positive).

Recovering technology. Given C with these properties, f(x)=\max\{y:\ w\cdot x\ge C(w,y)\ \forall w\gg0\} is increasing, unbounded and quasi-concave and generates C (isomorphic to Section 2.7); integrability also holds.

Example (Cobb–Douglas, f=x_1^\alpha x_2^\beta). x_1=\big(\tfrac{\alpha w_2}{\beta w_1}\big)^{\beta/(\alpha+\beta)}y^{1/(\alpha+\beta)}, cost C=A\,w_1^{\alpha/(\alpha+\beta)}w_2^{\beta/(\alpha+\beta)}y^{1/(\alpha+\beta)}; returns to scale are \alpha+\beta.

Worked example (cheapest way to produce 10). Take f(x_1,x_2)=\sqrt{x_1x_2} (\alpha=\beta=\tfrac12), input prices w=(1,4) and output y=10. The first-order condition MRTS=f_1/f_2=x_2/x_1=w_1/w_2=\tfrac14 gives x_1=4x_2. Then \sqrt{4x_2\cdot x_2}=2x_2=10, so x_2=5, x_1=20 and cost C=1\cdot20+4\cdot5=40. The formula agrees: C=2\sqrt{w_1w_2}\,y=2\cdot2\cdot10=40. Shephard's lemma: \partial C/\partial w_1=\sqrt{w_2/w_1}\,y=2\cdot10=20=x_1 ✓. Doubling both input prices doubles the cost to 80 (degree one). Marginal cost \partial C/\partial y=2\sqrt{w_1w_2}=4 is constant (constant returns).

4.4 Profit maximisation

\pi(p,w)=\max_{x\ge0}\ p\,f(x)-w\cdot x.

Warning: with constant or increasing returns the problem may have no solution (profit 0 or +\infty). First-order condition p\,f_i(x)=w_i: value of marginal product = input price.

Properties of the profit function: continuous; increasing in p, decreasing in w; homogeneous of degree one in (p,w); convex in (p,w); Hotelling's lemma: \partial\pi/\partial p=y(p,w) (output supply) and -\partial\pi/\partial w_i=x_i(p,w) (input demand).

Intuition for convexity. Opposite to the expenditure function: when prices change the firm can re-plan, so profit rises faster than linearly — profit is convex in prices.

Supply and demand properties: homogeneous of degree zero in (p,w); \partial y/\partial p\ge0 (law of supply), \partial x_i/\partial w_i\le0; the substitution matrix is symmetric and positive semi-definite (the opposite sign to the consumer's negative semi-definite Slutsky matrix), and integrability holds.

Worked example (profit maximisation). One input, f(x)=\sqrt x, output price p=4, input price w=1. Profit is 4\sqrt x-x; the first-order condition 2/\sqrt x=1 gives x=4, y=2, \pi=8-4=4. In general x=(p/2w)^2, y=p/(2w) and \pi(p,w)=p^2/(4w). Hotelling's lemma: \partial\pi/\partial p=p/(2w)=2=y ✓ and -\partial\pi/\partial w=p^2/(4w^2)=4=x ✓. Profit is convex in p (a parabola) and doubling p and w doubles \pi. With constant returns f(x)=x at p=4, w=1 every unit of input earns 3: profit is unbounded, the warning above.

4.5 Short run and long run

In the short run some inputs \bar x are fixed; short-run cost SC(w,\bar w,y;\bar x)=\min_x\ wx+\bar w\bar x s.t. f(x,\bar x)\ge y.

Theorem (marginal vs average). \dfrac{d}{dy}AVC=\dfrac{MC-AVC}{y}: AVC rises when MC>AVC and falls otherwise, so MC crosses AVC at its minimum (same for ATC).

Theorem (long vs short run). C(w,y)\le SC(w,\bar w,y;\bar x) for any fixed \bar x, with equality at the long-run optimal \bar x(w,y); by the envelope argument \dfrac{dC}{dy}=\dfrac{\partial SC}{\partial y} (long-run marginal cost equals the corresponding short-run marginal cost).

Shut-down. In the short run the firm stops producing when the price is below \min AVC (fixed cost is sunk; continuing would not even cover variable cost); in the long run it exits when the price is below \min ATC. Similarly \pi(p,w,\bar w;\bar x)\le\pi(p,w) with equality at the optimal fixed inputs.

Worked example (cost curves). Variable cost VC(y)=y^3-6y^2+14y and a fixed cost of 10. Then AVC=y^2-6y+14 is smallest at y=3, where AVC=5 and MC=3y^2-12y+14=5: MC crosses AVC at its minimum, as the theorem says. Average total cost ATC=AVC+10/y is smallest near y\approx3.43, where ATC\approx MC\approx8.1. So in the short run the firm shuts down if the price falls below 5 (it cannot even cover variable cost), but exits in the long run only if the price stays below about 8.1 (it cannot cover total cost). For prices between 5 and 8.1 it keeps producing at a loss in the short run, because the fixed cost is sunk.

4.6 Multi-product firms

Advanced section.

Describe Y by a transformation function F(y)\le0 with transformation frontier F(y)=0 and marginal rate of transformation MRT_{ij}=\dfrac{\partial F/\partial y_i}{\partial F/\partial y_j}=-\dfrac{dy_j}{dy_i}: how much of j must be given up for one more unit of i. Profit maximisation \max\,p\cdot y s.t. F(y)\le0 gives p_i/p_j=MRT_{ij} (price ratio = transformation rate, mirroring "price ratio = MRS" for consumers).

Theorem. If Y has non-decreasing returns, \pi(p)\le0 or \pi(p)=+\infty: once a plan earns positive profit, scaling it up earns unboundedly more.

5. General Equilibrium

Intuition. All earlier prices were "given". Where do they come from? General equilibrium answers: prices are the numbers that clear all markets simultaneously. One market's price affects demand in others, so they must be solved together. Walras's insight: the n market-clearing equations are not independent (Walras's law), so fixing relative prices leaves only n-1 independent equations. Arrow and Debreu then used fixed-point theorems to prove that under mild conditions such prices always exist.

5.1 The pure exchange economy

  • No production, only endowments e^i\in\mathbb R^n_+; private ownership; voluntary trade.
  • \mathcal E=\{(\succsim_i,e^i)\}_{i\in I}. An allocation x=(x^1,\dots,x^I) is feasible if \sum_ix^i=\sum_ie^i.
  • Preferences are complete, transitive, continuous and strictly convex.

With two consumers and two goods use the Edgeworth box: its width and height are the total amounts of the two goods; one agent's origin is bottom-left, the other's top-right. The contract curve is the set of points where the two indifference curves are tangent (no mutually beneficial trade remains). Individual rationality: x^i\succsim e^i.

5.2 Excess demand and Walras's law

At prices p\gg0 each agent solves \max U^i(x) s.t. p\cdot x\le p\cdot e^i. The excess demand for good k is z_k(p)=\sum_ix^i_k(p,p\cdot e^i)-\sum_ie^i_k; z(p)=(z_1,\dots,z_n).

Theorem. If utilities are continuous, strictly increasing and strictly quasi-concave:

  1. z(p) is continuous;
  2. homogeneous of degree zero (only relative prices matter);
  3. Walras's law p\cdot z(p)=0.

Proof (Walras). Each budget constraint reads \sum_kp_k[x^i_k-e^i_k]=0; sum over i and swap the order of summation to get \sum_kp_kz_k(p)=0. \square

Corollary. If n-1 of n markets clear, the last one does too.

Boundary behaviour (property 4). If p^m\to\bar p\ne0 with some \bar p_k=0, then some good k' with price tending to zero has unbounded excess demand ("if it is free, everyone wants it").

Proof idea. If excess demand were bounded, each agent's demands would have a convergent subsequence x^{i*}; a free good k could be taken in larger amounts at essentially no cost, and strict monotonicity plus continuity then give a strictly better affordable bundle near the end of the sequence, contradicting optimality. \square

Worked example (Alice and Bob trade). Two goods (apples and oranges), total supply (10,10). Both have U=\sqrt{x_1x_2}, so each spends half of wealth on each good. Endowments: Alice e^A=(8,2), Bob e^B=(2,8). Take good 2 as the numéraire (p_2=1) and let p be the price of good 1.

  • Alice's wealth is 8p+2: x^A=\big(\tfrac{8p+2}{2p},\ \tfrac{8p+2}{2}\big)=\big(4+\tfrac1p,\ 4p+1\big).
  • Bob's wealth is 2p+8: x^B=\big(1+\tfrac4p,\ p+4\big).
  • Excess demand for good 1: z_1(p)=(4+\tfrac1p)+(1+\tfrac4p)-10=\tfrac5p-5. For good 2: z_2(p)=(4p+1)+(p+4)-10=5p-5.
  • Walras's law: p\,z_1+z_2=5-5p+5p-5=0 for every p ✓.
  • Equilibrium: z_1=0\iff p^*=1, and then z_2=0 too. The allocation is x^A=x^B=(5,5); both are better off than at the start (U rises from \sqrt{8\cdot2}=4 to 5).

An auctioneer who announces p=0.5 sees z_1=5>0 and raises the price; at p=2, z_1=-2.5<0 and he lowers it: adjustment leads to p^*=1.

5.3 Existence of Walrasian equilibrium

Definition. p^*\gg0 is a Walrasian equilibrium if z(p^*)=0.

Lemma (Brouwer). A continuous map from a non-empty compact convex set S\subset\mathbb R^n to itself has a fixed point.

Theorem. If z(p) is continuous, satisfies Walras's law and the boundary condition, there is p^*\gg0 with z(p^*)=0.

In one sentence. Define a map "raise the price of goods in excess demand, lower the others"; Brouwer's theorem says a continuous map of the price simplex into itself has a fixed point, and a fixed point is a price vector with no excess demand.

Proof sketch (the "auctioneer" map).

  1. Restrict prices to the compact set S_\epsilon=\{p:\sum p_k=1,\ p_k\ge\epsilon/(1+2n)\} and truncate \bar z_k=\min(z_k,1).
  2. Define f_k(p)=\dfrac{\epsilon+p_k+\max\{0,\bar z_k(p)\}}{n\epsilon+1+\sum_m\max\{0,\bar z_m(p)\}}: goods in excess demand get a higher price, the rest are "diluted". It is continuous and maps the simplex into itself, so Brouwer gives a fixed point p^\epsilon.
  3. Let \epsilon\to0 and take a convergent subsequence p^\epsilon\to p^*. If some p_k^*=0, the boundary condition makes some excess demand unbounded, contradicting the fixed-point equation; so p^*\gg0.
  4. The limit equation p^*_k\sum_m\max\{0,\bar z_m\}=\max\{0,\bar z_k\}, multiplied by z_k(p^*) and summed with Walras's law, gives \sum_kz_k\max\{0,\bar z_k\}=0, so all z_k\le0; with p^*\cdot z=0 all are 0. \square

Intuition. The map is Walras's tâtonnement: raise prices of goods in excess demand, lower the others; a fixed point is a price vector that no longer changes.

5.4 Adding production

Advanced section: the idea is the same as in the exchange economy. See the worked example at its end.

Setup. Firm j's production set Y^j: ①contains 0; ②closed and bounded; ③strictly convex (ruling out CRS/increasing returns and ensuring a unique profit maximiser). Profit \pi^j(p)=\max_{y\in Y^j}p\cdot y; consumer i owns share \theta_{ij} of firm j, \sum_i\theta_{ij}=1.

Consumer's problem: \max U^i(x) s.t. p\cdot x\le p\cdot e^i+\sum_j\theta_{ij}\pi^j(p).

Aggregate profit maximisation. Maximising profit over Y=\sum_jY^j is equivalent to each firm maximising separately — firms do not interact, so they can be "summed".

Equilibrium: z(p)=\sum_i(x^i(p)-e^i)-\sum_jy^j(p)=0.

Existence. If some aggregate production y gives y+\sum e^i\gg0 (every good can be produced in positive amounts), there is p^*\gg0 with z(p^*)=0.

Proof point. Only the boundary behaviour needs checking. If a good is free at the limit price \bar p, total income \sum_im^i(\bar p)=\bar p\cdot(\sum e^i+y)>0, so someone has positive income and demands unboundedly much of the free good. \square

Worked example (Robinson Crusoe: one consumer, one firm). Robinson owns 3 hours and the only firm. The good c has price p=1 (numéraire); the wage is w. U=\sqrt{c\,\ell} with leisure \ell, so labour is n=3-\ell. The firm has f(n)=\sqrt n and maximises \sqrt n-wn: n=\dfrac1{4w^2}, y=\dfrac1{2w}, profit \pi=\dfrac1{4w}. Robinson's income is 3w+\pi and he spends half on leisure: w\ell=\tfrac12(3w+\pi). The labour market clears when 3-\ell=n, which gives w=\tfrac12. Then n=1, y=1, \pi=\tfrac12, income =2, \ell=2, c=1. Check: he works 3-2=1 hour, the firm uses 1 hour ✓; he eats the 1 unit produced ✓. The wage \tfrac12 equals the marginal product of labour f'(1)=\tfrac12 ✓.

6. The Welfare Theorems

Intuition. Are competitive markets "good"? The two fundamental theorems of welfare economics answer precisely. First theorem: under non-satiation, a competitive equilibrium is Pareto efficient — the invisible hand wastes nothing. Second theorem: any Pareto-efficient allocation, if preferences and technology are convex, can be achieved by redistributing initial wealth and then letting markets work — so efficiency and equity can be separated: redistribute first, then let markets operate.

6.1 Pareto optimality

The feasible set is F(e)=\{x:\sum x^i\le\sum e^i+\sum_jy^j\}. A feasible allocation is Pareto efficient if no other feasible allocation makes everyone at least as well off and someone strictly better off.

Blocking. A coalition S\subset I blocks x if there is x' feasible using only the coalition's resources with x'^i\succsim_ix^i for i\in S and strictly better for someone. The core is the set of unblocked feasible allocations. Core ⊂ Pareto efficient (the grand coalition is a coalition).

Utility possibility set U=\{\bar u:\ u_i(x^i)\ge\bar u_i,\ x\text{ feasible}\}; Pareto-efficient allocations correspond to its boundary (the utility frontier).

Solving for efficient allocations. If u_1 is strictly monotone, x^* is efficient iff it solves

\max\ u_1(x^1)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad u_i(x^i)\ge\bar u_i\ (i\ge2),\ \text{resource constraint}
for some feasible \bar u_i.

6.2 The social planner

With weights \lambda\gg0: \max\sum_i\lambda_iU_i(x^i) s.t. resources.

  • Sufficiency: a planner's solution is Pareto efficient (otherwise the weighted sum could be raised).
  • Necessity: if u_i are concave, the utility possibility set is convex; the supporting hyperplane theorem at a frontier point gives \lambda\ge0 maximised by it. (\lambda\ge0: if some \lambda_k<0, sending u_k\to-\infty makes the right side unbounded, a contradiction.)

Link to competitive equilibrium. The multiplier on the resource constraint is the competitive price; each agent's \lambda_iU_i' is proportional to prices. This is the mathematical core of the welfare theorems.

6.3 The first welfare theorem

Lemma (local non-satiation). If preferences are locally non-satiated and x^{i*} solves the consumer's problem, then x^i\succsim x^{i*}\Rightarrow p\cdot x^i\ge m_i and x^i\succ x^{i*}\Rightarrow p\cdot x^i>m_i.

Theorem (First Welfare Theorem). If preferences are locally non-satiated, every Walrasian equilibrium allocation is Pareto efficient.

In one sentence. A better allocation would have to cost more than the whole economy is worth at the equilibrium prices, so it cannot be feasible.

Proof. If a feasible (x,y) made everyone at least as well off and someone strictly better off, by the lemma everyone spends at least their income and someone strictly more, so \sum_ip^*x^i>\sum_ip^*e^i+\sum_jp^*y^{j*}. Since y^{j*} maximises profit, \sum_jp^*y^{j*}\ge\sum_jp^*y^j, hence \sum_ip^*x^i>\sum p^*e^i+\sum p^*y^j, contradicting feasibility priced at p^*. \square

Intuition. A better allocation must either cost more (unaffordable) or be affordable yet unchosen — both contradict each consumer being optimal within the budget. Note the theorem does not need convexity and says nothing about fairness.

Worked example (is Alice and Bob's equilibrium efficient?). At the starting point MRS^A=x_2/x_1=2/8=0.25 and MRS^B=8/2=4: Alice would give up a quarter of an orange for an apple, Bob would give four oranges for one apple, so there is plenty of room for trade. At the equilibrium (5,5),(5,5) both MRS equal 1, the price ratio: the indifference curves are tangent, no further trade helps anyone, and the allocation is Pareto efficient, as the first theorem says. In this economy the contract curve is the diagonal x^A_2=x^A_1, where MRS^A=MRS^B.

6.4 Core and equilibria: Edgeworth–Debreu–Scarf

Advanced section: it shows that competitive equilibrium is the only outcome of large-scale bargaining. It can be skipped.

Theorem. With locally non-satiated preferences, Walrasian equilibrium allocations are in the core (same argument: a blocking coalition would spend more than its total income).

Converse? The core is generally much larger than the set of equilibrium allocations. Consider the replica economy E_r with r identical consumers of each type (rI in total).

  • Equal treatment. With strictly convex preferences, members of a type receive the same bundle in the core of E_r. (If treatment within a type differed, the worst-off members of each type could pool, average the bundles and strictly improve.)
  • Shrinking core. r>r' ⟹ C_r\subset C_{r'}.
  • WEA lemma. Equilibrium allocations of E_r are exactly replicas of equilibrium allocations of E_1.

Edgeworth–Debreu–Scarf theorem. If x\in C_r for every r, then x is a Walrasian equilibrium allocation of E_1.

In one sentence. In a large replica economy any allocation that is not supported by prices is blocked by some small coalition, so only equilibrium allocations remain in the core.

Proof sketch.

  1. For all t\in[0,1], U^i((1-t)\tilde x^i+te^i)\le U^i(\tilde x^i). (Otherwise with t=1/r a coalition of r type-1 agents and r-1 of each other type could replace type 1's bundle by (1-t)\tilde x^1+te^1, which is feasible and strictly better for type 1, blocking \tilde x\in C_r.)
  2. So F(t)=U^i((1-t)\tilde x^i+te^i) peaks at t=0: \nabla U^i(\tilde x^i)\cdot(e^i-\tilde x^i)\le0. Efficiency equalises all MRS, so there is p\gg0 with \nabla U^i\propto p, hence p\tilde x^i\ge pe^i.
  3. Summing and using feasibility forces equality: p\tilde x^i=pe^i. \square

Intuition. As the economy gets larger, core points that are not equilibria are blocked by more and more small coalitions. Only allocations supported by prices survive. So competitive equilibrium is not a naive assumption but the inevitable outcome of coalitional bargaining in large economies.

6.5 The second welfare theorem

Definition (equilibrium with transfers). (x^*,y^*) and p^* form an equilibrium with transfers if there are wealth levels w_i with \sum_iw_i=p^*e+\sum_jp^*y^{j*}, firms maximise profit, consumers maximise utility subject to p^*x\le w_i, and the allocation is feasible. The transfer is T_i=w_i-[p^*e^i+\sum_j\theta_{ij}p^*y^{j*}].

A quasi-equilibrium replaces "x^i\succ x^{i*}\Rightarrow p^*x^i>w_i" with the weak "\ge", to handle boundary solutions.

Theorem (Second Welfare Theorem). Assume Y^j convex and preferences convex and locally non-satiated. Then for every Pareto-efficient (x^*,y^*) there is p^*\ne0 such that it is a quasi-equilibrium with transfers.

In one sentence. The bundles everyone prefers form a convex set that does not meet the convex set of feasible outcomes, so a line separates them, and the slope of that line is the price vector.

Proof in three steps.

  1. Aggregate. V_i=\{x:x\succ_ix^{i*}\} and V=\sum V_i are convex; so are Y=\sum_jY^j and Y+\{e\}.
  2. Separate. Efficiency implies (Y+\{e\})\cap V=\varnothing. The separating hyperplane theorem gives p\ne0 and r with pz\ge r on V and pz\le r on Y+\{e\}. Local non-satiation extends "\succ" to "\succsim", and feasibility gives r=p\sum x^{i*}=p(e+\sum y^{j*}).
  3. Decentralise. If x^k\succ_kx^{k*}, replacing agent k's bundle by x^k and everyone else's by x^{i*} lies in the closure of V, so px^k\ge px^{k*}. Similarly firms: py^j\le py^{j*}. \square

Theorem (quasi-equilibrium ⟹ competitive equilibrium). If some consumption vector is strictly cheaper than w_i ("cheaper point"), the quasi-equilibrium is a true competitive equilibrium. Corollary: this holds if w^i>0 for all i.

Intuition and message. Any socially desired efficient allocation can be reached through one-off wealth transfers plus letting prices do their work. Allocation and efficiency are "decoupled". But the transfers must be lump-sum (non-distortionary), and the government must be able to impose them — hard in practice, which is the root of the equity–efficiency trade-off in public economics.

Worked example (redistribute, then let markets work). Suppose society wants Alice to have more: the allocation x^A=(7,7), x^B=(3,3) lies on the contract curve, so it is efficient. The common MRS is 1, so the supporting prices are p=(1,1). At these prices Alice needs wealth 14 to afford (7,7) and Bob needs 6 for (3,3). Their endowments are worth 10 each, so a lump-sum transfer of 4 from Bob to Alice is needed. Each then maximises utility given the new wealth and chooses exactly (7,7) and (3,3) (half the wealth on each good). The market does the allocating; the transfer does the redistributing.

6.6 Applications and failures

Labour. Individuals choose (x^i,n^i) (with taste for leisure) subject to px^i\le pe^i+wn^i; firms maximise py-wn. Labour is just another good; the welfare theorems are unchanged.

Public goods and Lindahl equilibrium. A public good q is non-excludable and non-rival. If everyone faces the same price, free-riding appears. Lindahl's solution uses personalised prices r_i with \sum_ir_i equal to marginal cost — personalised commodities. Each person faces px^i+r_iq^d_i\le w_i, and market clearing requires q^d_i=q for all. The result satisfies the Samuelson condition \sum_iMRS_i=MRT. The catch: personalised prices need everyone's true preferences, and nobody has an incentive to tell the truth — exactly the problem mechanism design addresses.

Non-convex technology. With non-convex production sets (fixed costs, increasing returns) the second theorem may fail: an efficient allocation may not be decentralisable by prices. The generalisation is marginal-cost pricing p=\gamma_j\nabla F_j(y^{j*}), but firms may then make losses and need subsidies.

Worked example (a public good). A street light costs 8 per unit (MC=8). Alice's marginal benefit is MB_A=10-q and Bob's is MB_B=6-q. Efficient level (Samuelson): MB_A+MB_B=MC gives 16-2q=8, q=4. Private provision: Alice alone stops where MB_A=8, at q=2; Bob, who values the third unit at only 6-2=4<8, contributes nothing and free-rides, so 2 is below the efficient 4. Lindahl prices: at q=4 Alice's marginal benefit is 6 and Bob's is 2; charge exactly these personal prices (6+2=8=MC) and both demand q=4. The catch: the planner must know each MB, and each person would understate it to pay less (Chapter 11).

6.7 Time and uncertainty: Arrow–Debreu and Radner

Advanced section: it extends the theorems to time and risk by treating each date and state as a separate good.

State-contingent commodities. With L goods and S states, delivery of good l in state s is a separate commodity; a plan is x^i\in\mathbb R^{LS}. If preferences have an expected-utility form U_i(x^i)=\sum_s\pi_{si}U_i(x^i_s), the Arrow–Debreu equilibrium is just a Walrasian equilibrium of these LS commodities, with all markets opened at date 0.

Properties. If subjective probabilities agree across people (\pi_{si}/\pi_{s'i} independent of i), efficient allocations equalise MRS across states; and if aggregate resources in state s exceed those in s', prices satisfy p_{sn}/p_{s'n}<\pi_s/\pi_{s'} (goods are cheaper in resource-rich states).

Radner sequential equilibrium. Opening every market at date 0 is unrealistic. It suffices to trade one Arrow security (a way to transfer wealth across states) at date 0 and then trade in spot markets at date 1; each agent maximises subject to \sum_sq_sz_{si}\le0 and p_sx_{si}\le p_se^i_s+p_{1s}z_{si}.

Theorem (equivalence). Arrow–Debreu and Radner equilibria are equivalent: their budget sets coincide. Meaning: with enough securities (complete markets) "few markets opening repeatedly" produces the same allocation as "all markets opening once", and (by the first welfare theorem) nobody wants additional spot trades.

7. Static Games

Intuition. So far each agent was a "price taker": too small to affect prices. When players are few and affect each other (two firms setting prices, two countries negotiating, a few bidders in an auction), I must predict what you will do, and you must predict me. Game theory studies that mutual prediction. Its first key concept is the Nash equilibrium: nobody can gain by changing their own strategy alone.

7.1 Strategic-form games

G=\{N,S,u\}: players N=\{1,\dots,n\}, pure strategy sets S_i, payoff functions u_i:S\to\mathbb R. Zero-sum: \sum_iu_i(s)=0.

A mixed strategy \sigma_i\in\Sigma_i=\Delta(S_i) is a probability distribution on S_i (a simplex). The mixed extension \Gamma=\{N,\Sigma,U\} has expected payoffs U_i(\sigma)=\sum_s\prod_i\sigma_i(s_i)\,u_i(s).

Classic example (prisoner's dilemma):

Cooperate Defect
Cooperate 3, 3 0, 4
Defect 4, 0 1, 1

"Defect" is strictly dominant, so the only Nash equilibrium is (Defect, Defect) with payoffs (1,1), Pareto-dominated by (Cooperate, Cooperate). Individual rationality does not imply collective optimality.

7.2 Dominance

  • Strict dominance: \sigma_i is strictly dominated if some \sigma_i' gives U_i(\sigma_i',s_{-i})>U_i(\sigma_i,s_{-i}) for all s_{-i}; equivalently, for all mixed \sigma_{-i} (expectation is linear).
  • Weak dominance: never worse and strictly better in some case.
  • If a pure strategy s_i is dominated, any mixed strategy putting positive probability on s_i is dominated too.

Iterated deletion of strictly dominated strategies (IDSDS): the order does not matter. Iterated deletion of weakly dominated strategies (IDWDS): order can matter, and Nash equilibria may even be weakly dominated. So IDWDS is not used as a solution concept.

Worked example (iterated deletion). Payoffs (row, column):

L M R
T 1, 0 1, 2 0, 1
B 0, 3 0, 1 2, 0

Column's R is strictly dominated by M (2>1 against T, 1>0 against B): delete R. Now Row's B is strictly dominated by T (1>0 in both remaining columns): delete B. With only T left, Column chooses between L (payoff 0) and M (payoff 2): M. The unique survivor (T,M) is the Nash equilibrium, found without any guessing.

7.3 Nash equilibrium

Definition. \sigma^* is a Nash equilibrium if for every i and s_i'\in S_i: U_i(\sigma^*_i,\sigma^*_{-i})\ge U_i(s_i',\sigma^*_{-i}) (each strategy is a best response to the others).

Theorem (equivalent definition). A profile is a Nash equilibrium iff nobody has a profitable pure-strategy deviation. (A mixed deviation's payoff is an average of pure ones; if the average is profitable some pure strategy is.)

Theorem (indifference principle). If \sigma_i^* puts positive probability on both s_i and s_i', then U_i(s_i,\sigma_{-i}^*)=U_i(s_i',\sigma^*_{-i})\ge the payoff of every other pure strategy.

Intuition. You randomise only because you are indifferent among the options being mixed. A player's mixing probabilities are set by the opponent's payoffs (to make the opponent indifferent), not by the player's own.

Example (matching pennies, zero-sum). The row player wins 1 if the coins match. There is no pure equilibrium; the mixed one has both players at 1/2: if the column's probability differed from 1/2 some pure strategy would be strictly better for the row player.

Example (battle of the sexes): two pure equilibria and one mixed; a coordination game.

Existence (Nash). Every finite strategic-form game has a mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium.

In one sentence. Best responses form a non-empty, convex, closed-graph correspondence on the compact set of mixed profiles, so Kakutani's theorem gives a profile that is a best response to itself.

Proof. The best-response correspondence r(\sigma)=\times_ir_i(\sigma_{-i}) is: ①defined on the compact convex set \Sigma=\times\Delta(S_i); ②non-empty (a finite set has a maximum); ③convex-valued (a mixture of best responses is a best response since expectation is linear); ④closed-graph (upper hemicontinuous: if \tilde\sigma\notin r(\sigma) there is an \epsilon-better deviation, which persists along the sequence by continuity, a contradiction). Kakutani's fixed-point theorem gives \sigma^*\in r(\sigma^*). \square

How to find the equilibria of a small game (recipe). (1) For each opponent action, underline the player's best payoff. (2) A cell in which every payoff is underlined is a pure Nash equilibrium. (3) For a mixed equilibrium, choose each player's probabilities so that the other player is indifferent.

Worked example (battle of the sexes). Row and Column choose Opera (O) or Football (F):

O F
O 2, 1 0, 0
F 0, 0 1, 2

Pure equilibria: (O,O) and (F,F). Mixed: let Row play O with probability p. Column is indifferent when p\cdot1+(1-p)\cdot0=p\cdot0+(1-p)\cdot2, so p=\tfrac23. Let Column play O with probability q: Row is indifferent when 2q=1-q, so q=\tfrac13. Expected payoff in the mixed equilibrium: 2q=\tfrac23 for Row and p=\tfrac23 for Column, worse for both than either pure equilibrium, because they often miscoordinate.

Worked example (Cournot duopoly: a game with continuous strategies). Two firms choose quantities; the price is P=100-q_1-q_2 and the unit cost is 10. Firm 1's profit is (90-q_1-q_2)\,q_1. Setting its derivative to zero gives the best response q_1=\dfrac{90-q_2}{2}, and symmetrically q_2=\dfrac{90-q_1}{2}. The intersection is q_1=q_2=30, price 40, profit 30\cdot30=900 each. If they acted as one monopolist they would produce 45 in total (22.5 each, price 55, profit 1012.5 each): both would gain, but firm 1's best response to 22.5 is 33.75, so each wants to cheat. This is a prisoner's dilemma in quantities. With n symmetric firms each produces 90/(n+1): more competition pushes the price towards cost.

7.4 Rationalizability

Advanced section.

A strategy is never a best response if it is not a best response to any \sigma_{-i}. Strictly dominated strategies are never best responses; with two players the converse holds too (prove by constructing a Kakutani map). Rationalizability iteratively deletes never-best-response strategies.

Intuition. Rationalizability asks: "which strategies can be justified by some belief?" It is a looser cousin of Nash: Nash requires beliefs to be consistent and correct; rationalizability only requires each belief to be reasonable.

7.5 Correlated equilibrium

Advanced section.

Sometimes players need to coordinate (traffic lights). Public randomisation (sunspots): all players observe the same random variable z and strategies may depend on it. By randomising between two pure Nash equilibria one achieves any linear combination of their payoffs.

More generally take a correlation device \{\Omega,\pi,\{P_i\}\} where each player only sees their own information partition. A correlated strategy is p\in\Delta(\times S_i); obeying a recommended s_i must be optimal given the conditional distribution p(s_{-i}|s_i):

\sum_{s_{-i}}p(s_{-i}|s_i)u_i(s_i,s_{-i})\ge\sum_{s_{-i}}p(s_{-i}|s_i)u_i(s_i',s_{-i}).
This is a correlated equilibrium. The set of correlated equilibria is convex (defined by linear inequalities) and contains every mixed Nash equilibrium (as independent correlation), and one can maximise social welfare over it by linear programming.

8. Dynamic Games

Intuition. When moves are sequential a strategy must say not only "what do I do now" but "what would I do in every possible situation". This creates a new problem: non-credible threats. "If you do that I'll destroy us both" — if the time comes, I would not want to carry it out, so the threat is not credible. Subgame perfect equilibrium rules such threats out.

8.1 Extensive-form games

(N,A,X,Z,\iota,u): decision nodes X (histories), terminal nodes Z, players N, node ownership \iota:X\to N, feasible actions A(x), terminal payoffs u:Z\to\mathbb R^N. A pure strategy specifies an action at every node of the player, including ones never reached.

Imperfect information. Information sets group nodes the player cannot distinguish (same action set). Nature ("player 0") moves randomly with given probabilities. In perfect-information games all information sets are singletons.

Every extensive-form game has an associated strategic form.

8.2 Backward induction and subgame perfection

Backward induction (BI). In a finite perfect-information game, go from the last decision nodes backwards: the mover chooses the payoff-maximising action and the subtree is replaced by that payoff.

A proper subgame starts at a singleton information set whose successors' information sets also lie entirely after it. A subgame perfect equilibrium (SPE) induces a Nash equilibrium in every proper subgame. Inclusions: BI\subset SPE\subset NE.

Example (entry deterrence). An entrant moves first (Enter / Stay out); if it enters the incumbent chooses Fight or Accommodate. There are two Nash equilibria: (Stay out, Fight) and (Enter, Accommodate). The first rests on the threat of fighting, but once entry has occurred the incumbent prefers to accommodate — the threat is not credible, so it is not an SPE. The only SPE is (Enter, Accommodate).

Reading the numbers. The payoffs (entrant, incumbent) are (0,4) if the entrant stays out, (2,2) if it enters and the incumbent accommodates, and (-1,-1) if it enters and the incumbent fights. Backward induction: at the incumbent's node 2>-1, so it accommodates; the entrant, anticipating this, compares 2 (enter) with 0 (stay out) and enters. "(Stay out, Fight)" is a Nash equilibrium because, believing the threat, the entrant stays out and the fight is never put to the test; but it is not subgame perfect.

Mixed vs behavioural strategies. A mixed strategy randomises over complete plans; a behavioural strategy randomises independently at each information set. Under perfect recall (no one forgets what they knew) they are equivalent (Kuhn's theorem). Selten's theorem: every finite extensive-form game with perfect recall has an SPE.

8.3 The one-shot deviation principle

Intuition. To verify an SPE we cannot check all multi-step deviations. The one-shot deviation (OSD) principle says: it is enough to check one-step deviations — at every history, change only the current action (then follow the strategy) and see whether it pays.

Theorem (OSD). In a finite perfect-information game, s^* is an SPE iff there is no profitable one-shot deviation.

In one sentence. If a long profitable deviation existed, its last step alone would already be a profitable one-step deviation.

Proof (contrapositive, the non-trivial direction). If s^* is not an SPE a profitable multi-step deviation exists; take the one that differs from s^* in the fewest places. At the last history where it differs, it differs from s^* only in its first step and is strictly better — a profitable one-shot deviation. \square

Infinite horizon. OSD still holds if the game is continuous at infinity (the far future matters less and less). It must be checked at every history, on or off the path.

8.4 Rubinstein bargaining

Setup. Two players divide a pie of size 1. They alternate offers: player 1 proposes in even periods and player 2 in odd ones; the responder accepts (the game ends) or rejects (go to the next period, other player proposes). There is no deadline; perpetual disagreement pays 0. An agreement x=(x_1,x_2) reached at date t pays \delta_i^tx_i, \delta_i\in(0,1) the discount factor.

Too many Nash equilibria. For any \bar x, "always propose \bar x and accept only shares \ge\bar x_i" is a Nash equilibrium (almost any split can be supported). It relies on a non-credible threat: if the proposer offers slightly below \bar x_i I reject — but after rejecting I get at most \delta_i\bar x_i<\bar x_i, so at that history I should accept (exactly the off-path deviation OSD catches).

SPE. Require that accepting today's offer equals rejecting and proposing tomorrow:

y_1^*=\delta_1x_1^*,\qquad x_2^*=\delta_2y_2^*.
Solving,
x^*=\Big(\frac{1-\delta_2}{1-\delta_1\delta_2},\ \frac{\delta_2(1-\delta_1)}{1-\delta_1\delta_2}\Big),\quad y^*=\Big(\frac{\delta_1(1-\delta_2)}{1-\delta_1\delta_2},\ \frac{1-\delta_1}{1-\delta_1\delta_2}\Big).

Uniqueness. Let m_i,M_i be player i's lowest and highest SPE payoff in subgames where i proposes. The opponent rejects any offer below \delta_jm_j, so M_i\le1-\delta_jm_j, and accepts any offer above \delta_jM_j, so m_i\ge1-\delta_jM_j. Combining, M_i=m_i: the SPE is unique.

Conclusion. With \delta_1=\delta_2=\delta the first proposer gets \dfrac1{1+\delta}>\dfrac12 — a first-mover advantage; the more patient player gets more; as \delta\to1 the split tends to equal.

Worked example (splitting a pie). With \delta_1=\delta_2=0.9 the first proposer gets \dfrac{1-0.9}{1-0.81}=\dfrac{0.1}{0.19}\approx0.526 and the other 0.474. Check: if player 2 rejects, she proposes next period and gets 0.526, which is worth 0.9\times0.526=0.474 today, exactly what she is offered now, so she accepts. If player 2 is less patient, \delta_1=0.9, \delta_2=0.6, player 1 gets \dfrac{1-0.6}{1-0.54}=\dfrac{0.4}{0.46}\approx0.870. With \delta=0.5 for both the proposer gets \tfrac1{1.5}=\tfrac23; as \delta\to1 the split tends to 50{:}50.

8.5 Repeated games

Infinitely repeated game G(\infty): the stage game is played every period. With perfect monitoring all players see last period's action profile. A history is h^t=(a^0,\dots,a^{t-1}) and a strategy maps H\to A_i (or \Delta A_i). Average discounted payoff U_i(s)=(1-\delta)\sum_t\delta^tu_i(a^t(s)).

Automata. Strategies can be represented by finite machines (states W_i, initial state, output function f:W_i\to\Delta A_i, transition T:W_i\times A\to W_i).

Example (trigger strategy). In the repeated prisoner's dilemma: "cooperate until anyone defects, then defect forever". Cooperation is sustainable iff \dfrac{4-3}{4-1}\le\delta, i.e. \delta\ge1/3: the one-time gain from defection is 4-3=1, the per-period loss afterwards 3-1=2, discounted.

Folk theorem. The feasible set is F=\mathrm{conv}\{u(a)\} and player i's minmax payoff is \underline v_i=\min_{\sigma_{-i}}\max_{\sigma_i}U_i; any Nash payoff is at least \underline v_i. Let F^*=F\cap\{v:v_i\ge\underline v_i\} (feasible and individually rational). If F^* has non-empty interior, every v\in F^* can be supported by an SPE for all \delta\ge\delta_0 for some \delta_0<1.

Intuition. If players are patient enough, nearly any payoff better than the worst case is an equilibrium: make the punishment a (credible) minmax and the future gains from cooperation deter deviation. The cost: too many equilibria, so little predictive power.

Worked example (when does cooperation survive?). Repeat the prisoner's dilemma of Section 7.1 (3 for mutual cooperation, 4 for cheating a cooperator, 1 for mutual defection) for ever with discount factor \delta. Under the trigger strategy, cooperating for ever is worth 3+3\delta+3\delta^2+\dots=\dfrac3{1-\delta}. Cheating once yields 4 now and then 1 for ever: 4+\dfrac\delta{1-\delta}. Cooperation is an equilibrium if \dfrac3{1-\delta}\ge4+\dfrac\delta{1-\delta}, i.e. 3\ge4(1-\delta)+\delta=4-3\delta, i.e. \delta\ge\tfrac13. With \delta=0.9 cooperation is worth 30 and a single cheat only 4+9=13. Cooperation needs patience: the future must matter enough.

9. Games of Incomplete Information

Intuition. Until now players knew each other's payoffs. In reality I do not know your cost, your tastes or how smart you are. Harsanyi's insight: model "not knowing" as types — Nature first draws each player's type, each player knows only their own; uncertainty becomes beliefs about others' types. The game becomes an equilibrium of functions from types to actions.

9.1 Bayesian games and Bayes–Nash equilibrium

(N,S,\Theta,u,p): type spaces \Theta=\times\Theta_i, payoffs u_i(s;\theta), a joint prior p. A pure strategy is s_i:\Theta_i\to S_i. In a Bayes–Nash equilibrium (BNE) every type's action maximises its conditional expected payoff:

s_i(\theta_i)\in\arg\max_{\hat s_i}\sum_{\theta_{-i}}p(\theta_{-i}|\theta_i)\,u_i(\hat s_i,s_{-i}(\theta_{-i});\theta_i,\theta_{-i}).
Existence. Finite games have a mixed BNE; with continuous actions and types, continuous payoffs concave in own action, a pure BNE exists.

Worked example (a Bayesian Cournot game). The price is P=12-q_1-q_2 and firm 1 has cost 0. Firm 2 has cost 0 (type L) or 4 (type H), equally likely; only firm 2 knows its type. Firm 2's best responses are q_2^L=\dfrac{12-q_1}2 and q_2^H=\dfrac{8-q_1}2. Firm 1 does not know the type and maximises expected profit, so q_1=\dfrac{12-E[q_2]}2. Solving the three equations: q_1=\tfrac{14}3\approx4.67, q_2^L=\tfrac{11}3\approx3.67, q_2^H=\tfrac53\approx1.67. Check: E[q_2]=\tfrac83 and (12-\tfrac83)/2=\tfrac{14}3 ✓. Firm 2's strategy is a function of its type: that is what a Bayesian equilibrium is.

9.2 Refinements: PBE and sequential equilibrium

Advanced section: it makes precise what "credible beliefs" means. A first reading can go straight to signalling games.

In dynamic games of incomplete information Nash equilibria can still contain non-credible threats, and subgame perfection is not enough (information sets often do not start subgames). Beliefs must be written into the equilibrium.

An assessment (b,\mu) pairs behavioural strategies b with a system of beliefs \mu=(\mu_h)_{h\in H}, \mu_h\in\Delta(h): the probability of each node given that information set h is reached.

Perfect Bayesian equilibrium (PBE):

  1. Sequential rationality: at each information set the mover's strategy maximises continuation payoff given their belief;
