  2. Bayes' rule: whenever P(h|b)>0, \mu_h(x)=P(x|b)/P(h|b).

At off-path information sets (probability 0) PBE places no further restriction on beliefs (hence "weak PBE"), so sequential rationality can fail off path. PBE ⟹ NE.

Sequential equilibrium (SE): in addition to sequential rationality, beliefs must be consistent: there is a sequence of completely mixed behavioural strategies b_n\to b whose Bayes-induced beliefs \mu_n\to\mu. SE ⟹ PBE and SE ⟹ SPE; if every information set is reached on path, PBE = SE. (In general use SE, since its definition is uncontroversial.)

9.3 Signalling games

Setup. A sender has private type \theta\in\Theta (prior p) and chooses a message m\in M; the receiver observes m (not \theta) and chooses an action a\in A; payoffs u_S(m,a,\theta), u_R(m,a,\theta).

PBE. The sender is optimal for each type; the receiver is optimal after each message given beliefs \mu(\theta|m); beliefs follow Bayes' rule \mu(\theta|m)=\dfrac{p(\theta)\sigma(m|\theta)}{\sum_{\theta'}p(\theta')\sigma(m|\theta')} when the denominator is positive, and are arbitrary otherwise.

Separating equilibrium: different types send different messages, fully revealing the type; pooling equilibrium: different types send the same message.

Intuitive criterion. For an off-path message m, if some type \theta can never gain from sending m — whatever best response the receiver chooses — beyond its equilibrium payoff, call it a "sure loser" for m; the receiver's belief should put zero weight on it. If all types are sure losers, or none, the criterion is silent.

Intuition. "If you see a signal that only a good type could possibly want to send, why believe it came from a bad type?" This is a reasonableness requirement on off-path beliefs.

Worked example (Bayes' rule on a signal). A job applicant is "strong" with prior probability 30%. Strong applicants always send a costly signal; weak ones send it with probability 50%. After seeing the signal the employer's belief is

\mu(\text{strong}\mid\text{signal})=\frac{0.3\cdot1}{0.3\cdot1+0.7\cdot0.5}=\frac{0.3}{0.65}\approx0.46.
The signal raises the probability from 30% to 46% but proves nothing. In a pooling equilibrium (everyone sends it) it would not change the belief at all; in a separating equilibrium (only strong applicants send it) it would raise it to 100%.

Worked example (education as a signal). Productivity is 2 (high) or 1 (low), equally likely; the wage equals the employer's belief about productivity. Education e costs a high type e and a low type 2e (utility = wage - cost). In a separating equilibrium high types choose e^* and earn 2, low types choose 0 and earn 1. Low types do not mimic if 2-2e^*\le1, i.e. e^*\ge0.5; high types still prefer to signal if 2-e^*\ge1, i.e. e^*\le1. So every e^*\in[0.5,1] is a separating equilibrium, and the intuitive criterion selects the cheapest, e^*=0.5 (a higher level only wastes resources). High types then earn 1.5 and low types 1. In a pooling equilibrium (nobody studies, wage 1.5) both earn 1.5, but it fails the criterion: an applicant with e=0.4 would earn at most 2-0.4=1.6>1.5 if believed high, whereas a low type would get at most 2-0.8=1.2<1.5 and would never deviate. So the employer should believe "high", and the pooling equilibrium breaks.

10. Information Economics: Adverse Selection and Moral Hazard

Intuition. Asymmetric information comes in two basic forms. Adverse selection (hidden information): before the contract one side has private information (a buyer of insurance knows their risk better than the insurer). Moral hazard (hidden action): after the contract one side takes an action the other cannot see (once insured you may be less careful). Common conclusion: the optimal contract departs from the full-information optimum, creating information rents and efficiency loss.

10.1 The insurance model and adverse selection

Setup. All consumers have the same vNM utility u (continuous, strictly increasing, strictly concave); two states: good with wealth w, bad (loss) with wealth w-L; individuals differ in the bad-state probability \pi_i; insurers are risk neutral with no other costs. A contract (B,p): premium p, payout B if the loss occurs.

Full-information benchmark. Insurers observe \pi_i. Competition gives zero profit: p=\pi_iB. The consumer maximises \pi_iu(w-L-p+B)+(1-\pi_i)u(w-p) ⟹ B=L, p=\pi_iL. Full insurance; the risk-neutral insurer bears all risk; no market failure.

Asymmetric information. Insurers cannot observe \pi_i, only its distribution on [\underline\pi,\bar\pi]. Still B=L. Type \pi buys iff u(w-p)\ge\pi u(w-L)+(1-\pi)u(w), i.e. \pi>h(p) with

h(p)=\frac{u(w)-u(w-p)}{u(w)-u(w-L)}.
Only high-risk types buy, raising expected payouts: the equilibrium price satisfies p^*=E[\pi\mid\pi\ge h(p^*)]\,L (the adverse-selection "death spiral": higher price ⟹ low-risk types leave ⟹ average risk rises ⟹ price rises). An equilibrium exists (g(p)=E[\pi|\pi\ge h(p)]L is increasing and maps the interval into itself, so has a fixed point) but may be poor: low-risk types are priced out. This is Akerlof's "lemons market" in insurance form.

Worked example (the death spiral in numbers). Wealth 100; a loss of 100 (everything) hits with probability \pi: low-risk types \pi_L=0.1, high-risk types \pi_H=0.5, half each; U=\sqrt w. Full information: a low type pays 10 for full cover and has a sure wealth of 90, utility 9.49, above the 0.9\cdot10=9 she gets uninsured: she buys. Hidden information, one price: if everyone bought, the fair price would be the average risk, 0.3\times100=30. But at 30 a low type gets \sqrt{70}=8.37<9 and leaves. Only high types remain, so the fair price becomes 50; high types still buy (\sqrt{50}=7.07>5). The equilibrium has price 50 and only the high-risk insured: the low-risk market has vanished although a mutually beneficial price (10 for low types) exists.

10.2 Signalling: low-risk types prove themselves

Setup. Two consumer types \pi_L<\pi_H with utility U_i(B,p)=\pi_iu(W-L-p+B)+(1-\pi_i)u(W-p); the risk-neutral firm cannot see types; consumers propose a contract (B,p) and the firm accepts or rejects. Single-crossing: in the (B,p) plane the types' indifference curves cross only once (the high-risk type values coverage more, so its curve is steeper).

Benchmarks. High risk's full-information contract is (L,\pi_HL); the low type's outside option is the best contract if treated as high risk, (\tilde B_L,\pi_H\tilde B_L).

Separating PBE. The high type picks (L,\pi_HL); the low type picks (B_L,p_L) satisfying IR_L, IC_L (does not want to mimic the high type) and firm zero profit. The firm believes any other contract comes from the high type. The Riley outcome is the best separating equilibrium: IC_L binds (the low type is just indifferent to mimicking) and B_L<L (partial insurance): to prove its type, the low-risk consumer must buy less insurance.

Pooling PBE. Both types choose the same contract with zero profit p^*=\hat\pi B^*, \hat\pi=\alpha\pi_L+(1-\alpha)\pi_H. This requires \hat\pi not too large. If the low-risk share is high enough some pooling equilibria are strictly better than the best separating one.

Refinement by the intuitive criterion.

  • No pooling equilibrium satisfies the criterion: there is an off-path contract (B,p) profitable for the firm, strictly better for low risk and strictly worse for high risk — the high type is a sure loser, so the firm should believe it comes from the low type and accept it, breaking the pooling.
  • Only the Riley outcome satisfies the criterion.

10.3 Screening: the firm designs a menu

Setup. As above, but now firms (at least two, competing) offer a menu of contracts and consumers choose.

Theorem.

  1. Firms make zero profit in equilibrium: with positive profit a rival could skim by slightly raising payouts and take the whole market;
  2. There is no pooling equilibrium: any pooling contract can be broken by a contract attracting only low-risk types ("cream-skimming") and earning positive profit;
  3. The unique PBE is the Riley outcome (if it exists).

Intuition and contrast. In signalling the informed party moves; in screening the uninformed party moves. Both models give the same answer: low-risk types get only partial insurance — the price of asymmetric information.

10.4 Principal–agent: hidden type (two types)

Setup. A principal (firm) hires an agent (worker). The worker's cost type \theta\in\{\underline\theta,\bar\theta\} (efficient \underline\theta, inefficient \bar\theta) is private, with probability v of \underline\theta. The firm offers a menu (W,q) (wage, output); its payoff is S(q)-W (S concave); the worker earns W-\theta q with outside option 0.

Full information. Maximise S(q)-\theta q: S'(q)=\theta (efficient output).

Asymmetric information. Constraints: IR_H,IR_L,IC_H,IC_L (the efficient type wants to pretend to be inefficient). Logic:

  1. Monotonicity: IC_H+IC_L gives (\bar\theta-\underline\theta)(\bar q-\underline q)\le0: the higher-cost type produces less;
  2. IR_L (efficient type) is slack;
  3. IR_H (inefficient type) and IC_L (efficient type does not mimic) bind.

Solving:

S'(\underline q)=\underline\theta\quad(\text{efficient type: }\textbf{no distortion}),\qquad S'(\bar q)=\bar\theta+\frac{v}{1-v}(\bar\theta-\underline\theta)\quad(\text{inefficient type: output distorted down}).

Intuition. To make the efficient type tell the truth we must leave it an information rent U_L=(\bar\theta-\underline\theta)\bar q. The rent depends on the inefficient type's output \bar q, so the firm deliberately depresses \bar q to reduce the rent: a classic trade-off of efficiency for rent. "No distortion at the top" is a general result.

Worked example (the principal–agent menu). Take S(q)=2\sqrt q, costs \underline\theta=1 (efficient) and \bar\theta=2 (inefficient), each with probability \tfrac12 (so \tfrac v{1-v}=1).

  • Full information: S'(q)=1/\sqrt q=\theta gives \underline q=1, \bar q=\tfrac14; profit \tfrac12(2-1)+\tfrac12(1-\tfrac12)=0.75.
  • Hidden type: the efficient type is not distorted, \underline q=1. For the inefficient type S'(\bar q)=2+1\cdot(2-1)=3, so \bar q=\tfrac19.
  • Wages: the inefficient type gets zero surplus, \bar W=\bar\theta\bar q=\tfrac29. The efficient type must be left the rent (\bar\theta-\underline\theta)\bar q=\tfrac19, so \underline W=\underline\theta\underline q+\tfrac19=\tfrac{10}9.
  • Check: if the efficient type pretended to be inefficient he would produce \tfrac19 for \tfrac29 and earn \tfrac29-\tfrac19=\tfrac19, the same as telling the truth (\tfrac{10}9-1=\tfrac19): he is indifferent, so truth-telling is incentive compatible.
  • Profit: \tfrac12(2-\tfrac{10}9)+\tfrac12(\tfrac23-\tfrac29)=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac89+\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac49=\tfrac23\approx0.667, below 0.75: not knowing the type costs the principal 0.083.

10.5 Continuous types

Advanced section: the same logic as the two-type case, with an integral instead of a sum.

Setup. \theta\in[\underline\theta,\bar\theta] with density f and cdf F. Direct mechanism (W(\theta),q(\theta)).

Analysis.

  1. Local IC \theta=\arg\max_x\{W(x)-\theta q(x)\} gives W'(\theta)=\theta q'(\theta);
  2. Monotonicity q'(\theta)\le0 ensures the second-order condition;
  3. Integrating, U(\theta)-U(\tilde\theta)=-\int_{\tilde\theta}^\theta q(x)dx (information-rent formula: an efficient type's rent is the accumulated output of the less efficient types it could mimic);
  4. Local IC plus monotonicity gives global IC;
  5. Substitute IC and IR (U(\bar\theta)=0) into the objective and swap the order of integration:
    \max\int_{\underline\theta}^{\bar\theta}\Big[S(q(\theta))-\Big(\theta+\frac{F(\theta)}{f(\theta)}\Big)q(\theta)\Big]f(\theta)d\theta.
    Pointwise maximisation gives S'(q(\theta))=\theta+\dfrac{F(\theta)}{f(\theta)}, where \theta+F/f is the virtual cost. If F/f is increasing (a hazard-rate condition), q is monotone, satisfying the ignored constraint.

10.6 Moral hazard

Setup. The principal (insurer) is risk neutral; the agent (insured) is risk averse and dislikes effort e\in\{0,1\} with cost d(e). A loss l\in\{0,\dots,L\} occurs with probability \pi_l(e). The contract has premium p and payments B_l.

Monotone likelihood ratio property (MLRP): \pi_l(0)/\pi_l(1) is strictly increasing in l: the bigger the loss, the more it looks like no effort. It implies the loss distribution under e=0 first-order stochastically dominates that under e=1.

Full information. The principal observes e. For given e the optimal contract satisfies Borch's condition u'(w-p-l+B_l)=1/\lambda (constant) ⟹ B_l-l constant ⟹ full insurance (the risk-neutral principal bears all risk).

Moral hazard. An incentive-compatibility constraint is added: \sum\pi_l(e)u(\cdot)-d(e)\ge\sum\pi_l(e')u(\cdot)-d(e').

  • To induce e=0 the full-information contract is feasible directly.
  • To induce e=1 the first-order condition is
    \frac1{u'(w-p-l+B_l)}=\lambda+\Big(1-\frac{\pi_l(0)}{\pi_l(1)}\Big)\mu,
    with \lambda,\mu>0. Under MLRP, at loss levels with a high likelihood ratio (more likely no effort) the bracket is negative, so u' is larger — consumption is lower there: bad outcomes are linked to lower consumption as a punishment, so full insurance is not optimal.

Intuition. Full insurance removes the incentive to work ("someone will pay anyway"). To motivate effort the agent must bear some risk, which the risk-averse agent must be compensated for — the trade-off between risk sharing and incentives.

Continuous effort. a\in[0,1], success probability p(a) increasing and concave, effort cost c(a)=a. Replace IC by the first-order condition p'(a)(u(w_1)-u(w_0))=1 (the first-order approach), with second-order condition p''(a)(u(w_1)-u(w_0))<0 automatically satisfied. Result: the incentive multiplier \mu>0 and pay is sensitive to output: \dfrac{v'(1-w_1)}{u'(w_1)}=\lambda+\mu\dfrac{p'}{p}.

Worked example (moral hazard). An agent has u(w)=\sqrt w and can work (effort cost 1 in utility) or shirk. Success has probability 0.8 if she works and 0.4 if she shirks; she needs expected utility 3 to accept the job. Wages are w_1 (success) and w_0 (failure); write a=\sqrt{w_0}, b=\sqrt{w_1}. To make her work: 0.8b+0.2a-1\ge0.4b+0.6a, i.e. b-a\ge2.5. Participation: 0.8b+0.2a-1=3. With b=a+2.5 this gives a+2-1=3, so a=2, b=4.5: w_0=4, w_1=20.25, and the expected wage is 0.8\cdot20.25+0.2\cdot4=17. If effort could be observed, a sure wage with \sqrt w-1=3, i.e. w=16, would do. The difference 17-16=1 is the cost of the incentive: to motivate effort the agent must bear risk, and be paid a premium for it.

11. Mechanism Design

Intuition. Until now we analysed given rules (markets, auctions, contracts). Mechanism design reverses the question: if I am the rule-maker and want to achieve some goal (efficiency, maximal revenue), how should I design the rules? The difficulty: participants hold private information and will use the rules strategically. The revelation principle says we need not consider exotic rules; it suffices to consider "please report your type truthfully."

11.1 Auctions

Second-price (Vickrey) auction. The highest bidder wins and pays the second-highest bid.

Theorem. Bidding one's value b_i=v_i weakly dominates every other strategy.

Intuition. Your bid only determines whether you win, not what you pay (you pay someone else's bid). Bidding above v_i only adds the chance of winning a losing deal (when the top rival bid lies between v_i and your bid); bidding below v_i only forgoes a profitable win. Truth-telling loses on neither side.

Proof. Compare b_i<v_i with b_i=v_i: if the top rival bid B_{-i}<b_i or B_{-i}>v_i the outcomes coincide; if b_i\le B_{-i}<v_i, bidding the value wins at profit v_i-B_{-i}>0 whereas underbidding loses it or splits ties. The case b_i>v_i is symmetric. \square

First-price auction. The highest bidder wins and pays their own bid. Suppose n bidders with i.i.d. valuations with cdf F on [0,1] and a strictly increasing differentiable equilibrium bid b(v). A type v mimicking r has expected payoff F(r)^{n-1}(v-b(r)) with first-order condition \dfrac{d}{dv}\big[G(v)b(v)\big]=g(v)v (G=F^{n-1}). Integrating,

b(v)=E\big[\max_{j\ne i}v_j\ \big|\ \max_{j\ne i}v_j<v\big].
That is, bid = expected second-highest value given that I am the highest.

Example (uniform): F(v)=v gives b(v)=\dfrac{n-1}nv: the more bidders, the closer to the true value.

The seller's expected revenue is the same in both auctions — a special case of revenue equivalence below.

Worked example (auctions with numbers). Values v=(70,50,30). Second-price: everyone bids their value, bidder 1 wins and pays 50, earning 70-50=20. Had she bid 40 she would lose and earn 0; had she bid 100 she would still pay 50. Bidding differently never helps.

First-price with two bidders, values uniform on [0,1]: bid b=v/2. A bidder with v=0.8 bids 0.4; she wins if the rival's bid is lower, i.e. if the rival's value is below 0.8 (probability 0.8), so her expected profit is 0.8\times(0.8-0.4)=0.32. Generally a bid b wins with probability 2b and earns 2b(0.8-b), which is largest at b=0.4. Bidding 0.5 wins for sure but earns only 0.3.

Revenue equivalence: second-price revenue is the expected lower value, \tfrac13. First-price revenue: the winner has the higher value (expected \tfrac23) and pays half of it, \tfrac13. Same.

11.2 Mechanisms and the revelation principle

Setup. One indivisible good, N risk-neutral buyers with private values v_i\in\Theta_i (independent; distributions F_i are common knowledge). A buyer gets v_i-p if she receives the good and -p otherwise.

A mechanism (S_i,P_i,C_i) has strategy spaces S_i, winning probabilities P_i(s) (\sum_iP_i\le1) and expected payments C_i(s). It is a direct mechanism if S_i=\Theta_i. A truthful BNE has everyone reporting their true type.

Revelation principle. For every BNE of any mechanism there is an equivalent truthful BNE of a direct mechanism (same winning probabilities and payments).

In one sentence. A mediator can play your equilibrium strategy for you; so if you tell her your true type you do exactly as well as in the original mechanism.

Proof. Construct the direct mechanism \hat P_i(v)=P(\sigma^*(v)), \hat C(v)=C(\sigma^*(v)) — "play the original equilibrium strategy on your behalf". The BNE inequalities of the original mechanism translate exactly into truthful reporting being optimal in the direct mechanism. \square

Intuition and significance. This simplifies design enormously: it suffices to search among truthful direct mechanisms instead of enumerating every conceivable auction format.

11.3 Incentive-compatible direct selling mechanisms

Notation. If others report truthfully and i reports r: interim winning probability \bar P_i(r)=\int P_i(r,v_{-i})dv_{-i}, expected payment \bar C_i(r), and expected payoff U_i(r,v_i)=\bar P_i(r)v_i-\bar C_i(r).

Theorem (characterisation of IC). A direct mechanism is incentive compatible iff:

  1. \bar P_i(\cdot) is non-decreasing;
  2. \bar C_i(v_i)=\bar C_i(0)+\bar P_i(v_i)v_i-\int_0^{v_i}\bar P_i(x)dx.

Proof. ① Adding U(v,v)\ge U(\tilde v,v) and U(\tilde v,\tilde v)\ge U(v,\tilde v) gives (v-\tilde v)(\bar P(v)-\bar P(\tilde v))\ge0. ② The local IC first-order condition \bar P'(v)v=\bar C'(v) integrates to the formula; monotonicity gives the second-order condition. \square

Revenue equivalence. If two mechanisms have truthful BNE with the same \bar C(0) and the same \bar P_i(v_i), the seller's expected revenue is the same. (Revenue is \sum_i\int\bar C_i(v_i)f_i(v_i)dv_i, and by the formula \bar C is determined by \bar P and \bar C(0).)

Implication: as long as the auction "gives the good to the highest-valued bidder" and "the lowest type earns zero surplus", first-price, second-price and all-pay auctions give the same expected revenue — the format itself is irrelevant.

11.4 Optimal auctions (Myerson)

Virtual valuation: \psi_i(v_i)=v_i-\dfrac{1-F_i(v_i)}{f_i(v_i)}. Regularity: \psi_i is increasing.

Substituting the IC formula into the seller's expected revenue and swapping integrals gives

E[R]=\sum_i\int\bar P_i(v_i)\,\psi_i(v_i)\,f_i(v_i)\,dv_i=E\Big[\sum_iP_i(v)\psi_i(v_i)\Big].

Intuition. Revenue equals the expected virtual valuation of the winner. Virtual valuation = value minus the information-rent term \dfrac{1-F}{f}: leaving one more dollar of rent to type v means leaving it to all higher types too, so the rent term is multiplied by the mass of higher types.

Myerson's theorem. Under IR and \bar C_i(0)=0 the optimal mechanism gives the good to the bidder with the highest and positive virtual valuation, otherwise it is not sold:

P_i(v)=1\ \text{if}\ \psi_i(v_i)>\psi_j(v_j)\ (j\ne i)\ \text{and}\ \psi_i(v_i)>0.
Regularity makes \bar P_i monotone, hence IC. Payments can follow the canonical payment rule C_i(v)=P_i(v)v_i-\int_0^{v_i}P_i(x,v_{-i})dx.

Example (uniform, n symmetric bidders). \psi(v)=2v-1, so \psi>0\iff v>1/2: the optimal auction is a second-price auction with reserve price 1/2. The reserve sometimes prevents a sale (an efficiency loss) but raises revenue. Optimal ≠ efficient: to extract rent the seller deliberately creates inefficiency.

Worked example (the optimal reserve with two bidders). Values uniform on [0,1], \psi(v)=2v-1, reserve price \tfrac12. Both values below \tfrac12 (probability \tfrac14): no sale, revenue 0. Exactly one above (probability \tfrac12): sale at the reserve \tfrac12. Both above (probability \tfrac14): sale at the lower value, whose expected value is \tfrac12+\tfrac16=\tfrac23. Revenue =\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12+\tfrac14\cdot\tfrac23=\tfrac5{12}\approx0.417, against \tfrac13 with no reserve. Revenue rises, but with probability \tfrac14 the good stays unsold although both buyers value it: the efficiency cost of optimality.

The structure of the whole subject in one table:

Level Question Core concepts Key theorems
Individual choice How does one agent choose optimally preferences, utility, budget, duality utility existence; Roy, Shephard; Slutsky; integrability
Uncertainty How to choose under risk vNM utility, risk aversion expected utility theorem; Arrow–Pratt; FOSD/SOSD
Firms How to produce and price production set, cost, profit properties of cost/profit functions; Hotelling

Welfare Is equilibrium good Pareto, core the two welfare theorems; EDS theorem

Ideas to take away:

  • Optimisation + duality + the envelope theorem is the basic recipe for deriving testable implications from individual theory: all the "lemmas" (Roy, Shephard, Hotelling) are the same envelope theorem.
  • Convexity is the key to the welfare theorems: it lets a price system "support" an allocation. Non-convexity (increasing returns, fixed costs, public goods) causes failure.
  • Credibility is the core of dynamic games: threats and promises must be optimal at every history — and one-shot deviation is the quickest check.
  • Information is valuable and costly: asymmetric information creates rents, distortions and market failure; signalling, screening and mechanism design are the remedies.
  • Truth-telling can be designed: the revelation principle gives the right target, and incentive compatibility makes it implementable.

13. Common Misconceptions

Misconception Correct
Utility numbers measure happiness In consumer theory only the ranking matters (any increasing transformation is equivalent); only in expected utility do the numbers matter, and then only up to a positive affine transformation
A good with an upward-sloping demand curve is "Giffen" by definition A Giffen good must be inferior and its income effect must outweigh the substitution effect; the substitution effect itself always lowers demand
Marshallian and Hicksian demand are the same They coincide only at the base prices; away from them they differ by the income effect
Risk-averse people never gamble They demand a premium; they accept any gamble whose expected gain exceeds their risk premium
A competitive equilibrium is fair The first welfare theorem says it is efficient, nothing about distribution; the second says distribution can be chosen by lump-sum transfers
Walras's law means all markets clear automatically It says the value of excess demands is zero, so if n-1 markets clear the last does; prices must still be found
A Nash equilibrium is a good outcome It may be Pareto-dominated (prisoner's dilemma, Cournot)
A mixed equilibrium means players flip coins because they are indifferent for themselves Each player's probabilities make the opponent indifferent
Every Nash equilibrium of a sequential game is credible Only subgame perfect equilibria rule out empty threats
The folk theorem says repeated play produces cooperation It says cooperation can be an equilibrium for patient players, and so can almost everything else: little predictive power
Asymmetric information always destroys a market It distorts it (partial insurance, rents, reserve prices); only in the extreme does the market unravel
The first-price auction raises more because bids are higher Bidders shade their bids; with independent private values revenue is the same as in the second-price auction
Restricting attention to truth-telling mechanisms loses generality The revelation principle says it loses nothing

14. Exercises with Answers

1. Does V=\ln x_1+\ln x_2 represent the same preferences as U=\sqrt{x_1x_2}? Does W=x_1+x_2?

Answer. V=2\ln U is an increasing transformation of U, so yes. W does not: U(4,1)=U(2,2)=2 (indifferent) but W(4,1)=5\ne W(2,2)=4.

2. A consumer has U=x_1^{0.3}x_2^{0.7}, income 200 and prices p=(3,7). Find the demand, and the demand if income doubles.

Answer. x_1=0.3\cdot200/3=20, x_2=0.7\cdot200/7=20 (budget shares 30% and 70%). At income 400 both double: (40,40).

3. In Exercise 2 the price of good 1 rises to 4.5 (50% more). Find the new demand for both goods. What happens to spending on good 2?

Answer. x_1=0.3\cdot200/4.5=13.33 (down by 6.67); x_2=0.7\cdot200/7=20 is unchanged. With Cobb–Douglas preferences budget shares are constant, so the cross-price effect on good 2 is zero (the substitution and income effects cancel).

4. Check WARP: at p^1=(1,1) the choice is x^1=(3,1); at p^2=(1,2) it is x^2=(1,2).

Answer. At p^1: x^1 costs 4, x^2 costs 3, so x^2 was affordable and x^1 is revealed preferred. WARP then requires p^2x^1>p^2x^2. But p^2x^1=3+2=5 and p^2x^2=1+4=5: not strictly greater. WARP is violated.

5. u=\ln w and a 50–50 gamble on wealth 50 or 200. Find the certainty equivalent and the risk premium.

Answer. E[u]=\tfrac12\ln50+\tfrac12\ln200=\tfrac12\ln10000=\ln100, so CE=100. E[w]=125, premium =25.

6. Show that an expected-utility maximiser cannot choose A in the first Allais choice and D in the second (Section 3.2).

Answer. A\succB gives 0.11U(1)>0.1U(5)+0.01U(0). D\succC gives 0.1U(5)+0.9U(0)>0.11U(1)+0.89U(0), i.e. 0.1U(5)+0.01U(0)>0.11U(1). The two inequalities contradict each other.

7. f=\sqrt{x_1x_2}, input prices w=(4,9), output 6. Find the cost-minimising inputs and the cost.

Answer. x_2/x_1=w_1/w_2=4/9, so x_2=\tfrac49x_1; \sqrt{x_1\cdot\tfrac49x_1}=\tfrac23x_1=6, so x_1=9, x_2=4, C=4\cdot9+9\cdot4=72. Formula: 2\sqrt{36}\cdot6=72 ✓.

8. f(x)=\sqrt x, p=8, w=2. Find the input demand, the supply and the profit, and check Hotelling's lemma.

Answer. 8/(2\sqrt x)=2 gives x=4, y=2, \pi=16-8=8=p^2/(4w). Hotelling: \partial\pi/\partial p=p/(2w)=2=y ✓.

9. Alice has e^A=(4,0) and Bob e^B=(0,4); both have U=\sqrt{x_1x_2}. Find the equilibrium price of good 1 (good 2 is the numéraire) and the allocation.

Answer. Alice's wealth is 4p: x^A=(2,2p). Bob's wealth is 4: x^B=(2/p,2). Good 1: 2+2/p=4 gives p=1. Allocation (2,2) each. Check good 2: 2p+2=4 ✓.

10. In Alice and Bob's economy of Section 5.2 (e^A=(8,2), e^B=(2,8)) society wants x^A=(6,6), x^B=(4,4). Is it efficient? Which prices and which transfer support it?

Answer. Both MRS equal 1, so it is on the contract curve and efficient. Supporting prices p=(1,1); wealth needed: Alice 12, Bob 8; endowments are worth 10 each, so Bob transfers 2 to Alice.

11. Find all Nash equilibria: Row's payoffs/Column's payoffs in cells (U,L) 3,1; (U,R) 0,0; (D,L) 0,0; (D,R) 1,3.

Answer. Pure: (U,L) and (D,R). Mixed: Row plays U with probability p such that Column is indifferent: p=3(1-p), p=\tfrac34. Column plays L with probability q such that Row is indifferent: 3q=1-q, q=\tfrac14. Payoffs \tfrac34 each.

12. Cournot with n=3 identical firms, P=100-Q, cost 10. Find the output, price and profit per firm.

Answer. q=90/(n+1)=22.5, Q=67.5, P=32.5, profit =(32.5-10)\cdot22.5=506.25 (compare 900 each with n=2).

13. Rubinstein bargaining with \delta_1=0.8, \delta_2=0.5. What does the first proposer (player 1) get?

Answer. \dfrac{1-\delta_2}{1-\delta_1\delta_2}=\dfrac{0.5}{0.6}=\dfrac56.

14. Principal–agent with S(q)=2\sqrt q, \underline\theta=1, \bar\theta=3, v=\tfrac12. Find the output of each type and the efficient type's rent.

Answer. Efficient type: S'(q)=1 gives \underline q=1. Inefficient type: S'(\bar q)=3+1\cdot(3-1)=5, 1/\sqrt{\bar q}=5, \bar q=\tfrac1{25}=0.04. Rent =(\bar\theta-\underline\theta)\bar q=2\cdot0.04=0.08.

15. Glossary

Term Meaning
Preference relation \succsim a person's ranking of options ("at least as good as")
Utility function a number attached to each option so that a higher number means a better option
Indifference curve all bundles that are equally good
Marginal rate of substitution (MRS) how much of one good one will give up for one more unit of another
Marshallian demand what the consumer buys at given prices and income
Hicksian (compensated) demand what the consumer buys to reach a given utility at least cost
Indirect utility V(p,I) the best utility reachable with income I at prices p
Expenditure function e(p,U) the least money needed to reach utility U at prices p
Duality the fact that "best utility for a budget" and "cheapest budget for a utility" describe the same choice
Substitution / income effect the parts of a demand change due to relative prices / to purchasing power
Normal / inferior / Giffen good demand rises / falls with income / rises with its own price
Revealed preference (WARP) inferring preferences from choices; WARP rules out contradictory choices
Lottery a list of outcomes with probabilities
von Neumann–Morgenstern utility a utility under which a lottery is valued at its expected utility
Certainty equivalent / risk premium the sure amount equivalent to a gamble / expected value minus that amount
Stochastic dominance a gamble that every (increasing, or increasing concave) utility prefers
Production set all feasible input–output plans of a firm
Returns to scale how output changes when all inputs are scaled
Cost / profit function least cost of an output / maximal profit at given prices
Shephard / Hotelling lemma the derivative of cost (profit) in a price is the input (output) quantity
Walrasian equilibrium prices at which every market clears while everyone optimises
Excess demand demand minus supply of a good at given prices
Numéraire the good whose price is set to 1, so other prices are relative
Walras's law the value of all excess demands is zero
Edgeworth box a diagram of a two-person, two-good exchange economy
Pareto efficient no one can be made better off without making someone worse off
Core allocations no group of people can improve on by itself
Contract curve the Pareto-efficient points of an Edgeworth box
Lump-sum transfer a transfer that does not depend on anything the person does
Public good non-excludable and non-rival (a street light)
Lindahl prices personalised prices for a public good that sum to its cost
Nash equilibrium a strategy profile in which each strategy is a best response to the others
Dominant strategy a strategy that is best whatever the others do
Mixed strategy a probability distribution over pure strategies
Subgame perfect equilibrium (SPE) a Nash equilibrium in every subgame; no empty threats
Backward induction solving a game from its last move to its first
Folk theorem with enough patience, any feasible payoff above the minmax can be an equilibrium of the repeated game
Type a player's private information (cost, taste, skill)
Bayes–Nash equilibrium each type's strategy is optimal given beliefs about the others' types
Perfect Bayesian equilibrium (PBE) strategies optimal given beliefs, and beliefs follow Bayes' rule on the path
Signalling / screening the informed party acts to reveal its type / the uninformed party offers a menu
Pooling / separating equilibrium all types act alike / different types act differently
Adverse selection hidden information before the contract: the worst types are the ones who buy
Moral hazard hidden action after the contract
Information rent the surplus that a better type must be left to tell the truth
Incentive compatibility (IC) telling the truth is optimal for every type
Individual rationality (IR) the participant prefers joining to the outside option
Revelation principle any equilibrium outcome of any mechanism can be obtained by a truthful direct mechanism
Virtual valuation v-\frac{1-F(v)}{f(v)}: a bidder's value net of the rent that must be left to higher types
Reserve price the lowest price at which the seller will sell
